Evidence strength: weak on revenue.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: A statute (GENIUS Act, 2025), an exchange designation plus litigation (Kalshi, CFTC-regulated since 2020 per Sacra), a rulemaking (Part 108, pending).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Banks and brokers could not offer products the law banned; Intrade was offshore and ran afoul of the CFTC; Libra/Diem's backers could not obtain regulatory sign-off.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Prediction markets: open but getting crowded (Polymarket US, Robinhood) and legally fragile because sports are ~80% of volume and states are suing. Stablecoin issuance is dominated by Circle/Tether; open space is the rails around it. Drones: pre-unlock.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: categories where a named regulator has signaled yes but only one or two licensed entrants exist (regulated event contracts on non-sports data; tokenized versions of existing securities/treasury products; B2B cross-border flows on dollar tokens; anything waiting on a federal rule with a published deadline). Price the legal premise first (lessons.md item 4): a state-by-state fight can erase the pool.

patterns.name: A government payer code or compliance mandate creates the budget line a product never had
patterns.mechanism: Products that work but have no payer die. When government creates a billing code or a legal duty, it creates a buyer with a budget line. Risks: codes are barely used, or mandates are unenforced or delayed.

examples.company: Pear Therapeutics (dead 2023) / CMS digital mental health treatment codes
examples.evidence: Pear filed Ch.11 Apr 2023: only about half of prescriptions were covered by insurers, could not raise in 2022-Q1 2023, laid off 170 (92%). CMS created G0552-G0554 in the CY2025 fee schedule and widened them for CY2026; G0552 still contractor-priced; analysts say claim volume is low. NO revenue evidence found.

SCOTUS upheld Texas age verification 6-3 (Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, Jun 2025); UK Online Safety Act enforced (children meeting 'highly effective' checks 25% to 43%, Jul 2025-Jan 2026; GBP 1.35M fine Feb 2026); Australia under-16 ban in force 10 Dec 2025 but testers opened accounts on 9 of 10 platforms with no proof asked. Persona $200M Series D at $2B (Apr 2025, no revenue disclosed); k-ID $45M Series A; Yoti revenue only GBP 6.2M in FY to Mar 2023; >50 firms bid for Australia's tech. Evidence strength: WEAK.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: A dated administrative act (CMS final rule) or court ruling/statute creating a payer or a duty.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Platforms had no duty to verify; payers had no code to pay.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Age assurance is already crowded with funded vendors, falling per-check prices and weak enforcement; payer-code products show little revenue. Weakest pattern for a $100M bottom-up path unless a mandate comes with enforcement and a fixed fee per user.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES to verify: other new mandates with a deadline, a fine schedule and a named compliance owner (e.g., CMS prior-authorization API requirements running into 2027, e-invoicing mandates in Europe; both UNVERIFIED in this run). Check each rule's date, penalties and delay history.

patterns.name: A scarce licensed asset is re-rated when a new use-case arrives
patterns.mechanism: A license (spectrum, permit, slot, right-of-way) is worth little under its old use and a lot under a new one. First owners fail or sit on it; the asset is later sold or leased at a multiple to whoever has the new platform.

examples.evidence: FCC moved to block LightSquared in Feb 2012 over GPS interference; Ch.11 May 2012. EchoStar agreed to sell AWS-4 + H-block (65 MHz) to SpaceX for ~$17B (~$8.5B cash + $8.5B stock + ~$2B interest payments); FCC approved 12 May 2026; close expected by Nov 2027.

80+ year rights to up to 40 MHz of L-band (~$550M at closing, ~$80M/yr, 4.7M penny warrants; court approved 23 Jun 2025). Revenue FY2025 $70.9M, Q1 2026 $14.7M, Q2 2026 ~$31.5M, FY2026 guide $150-200M; commercial service slipped to 2027; BlueBird 7 reached too-low an orbit in Apr 2026 and was de-orbited. Revenue still small vs price paid for spectrum.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Cheap launch and large phased-array satellites made space-to-phone service viable; the FCC reframed the band's use.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: LightSquared could not make terrestrial LTE coexist with GPS; EchoStar's own terrestrial wireless build did not pay off (background, unverified); the new use belonged to a different industry.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: The big spectrum prizes are taken (SpaceX, AT&T, AST). The pattern stays open for any scarce license whose best use has changed.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: stranded licensed or permitted assets whose best use shifted due to AI power demand or electrification: grid-interconnection positions at closed power plants, brownfield sites with transmission access, water rights near industrial clusters, rights-of-way/conduit, airport and port slots. A buy-side aggregator or broker with a data edge is a services-to-asset wedge. Needs pool sizing and a transferability legal check.

patterns.name: A cost input falls ~10x because someone else scaled; the owner of the cost curve captures the category
patterns.mechanism: A category looks absurd at 10x the cost, and first-wave startups die on the capital and launch bill. A different player drives the input cost down for its own reasons and enters the category already holding the cheap input.

examples.evidence: 2025 Starlink revenue $11.4B (+49.8%), segment operating income $4.4B (39% margin), capex $4.2B, subscribers 2.3M (2023) to 8.9M (2025) to 10.3M (31 Mar 2026), ~9,600 satellites; ARPU down ~18% 2023-2025 as it moved into cheaper markets (secondary summary of the S-1). OneWeb filed Ch.11 27 Mar 2020 with 74 of 648 satellites launched after SoftBank funding failed.

Dec 2025 survey: avg pack price $108/kWh (record low); stationary-storage packs $70/kWh (-45% vs 2024), driven by Chinese cell overcapacity (557 GWh stationary cells made vs about half that installed). Grid battery installs 112 GW (BNEF) / 108 GW (IEA) in 2025, ~10x in four years; BNEF forecasts 158 GW in 2026.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Reusable rockets (SpaceX, background) and Chinese manufacturing overcapacity in cells (2023-2025).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Pre-Starlink constellations had no control of launch cost; the cost curve belonged to a rival or to a foreign industry.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Satellite broadband is effectively closed to new entrants. Storage is open for integrators and software, but overcapacity-driven price collapse thins margins for Western manufacturers, and round 1 already found energy niches too small.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: look for finished-goods categories uneconomic only because one input is ~10x too dear, where that input already falls on someone else's curve (sensors, batteries, compute, actuators, satellite bandwidth); be the integrator/distributor downstream, not the upstream manufacturer. Candidate pools to size: storage-plus-load integration for commercial buildings and data centers; any service priced per kWh or per GB that could be cut ~80%.

patterns.name: A deep-pocketed buyer's demand shock (AI buildout) re-rates a stalled supply technology
patterns.mechanism: When a buyer with enormous capex hits a hard bottleneck (power, inference speed), it pays a premium for any supplier who can deliver now. Technologies stuck in pilot mode for a decade suddenly have a customer whose problem is speed, not price.

examples.evidence: 2025 revenue $2.02B (+37%), GM 29.0%; Q2 2026 revenue $1,065.4M (+165.5%), GAAP GM 33.4%; FY2026 guide raised to $3.9-4.2B; CEO: all major US hyperscalers and over a dozen neoclouds/AI labs approved its power systems. Backlog ~$20B at YE2025 (~$6B product, ~$14B service contracts cancelable annually; from Q4-25 release, not in the Q2 8-K).

IPO 14 May 2026 raised ~$2.2B; revenue tiny (Q1 2026 $61k, Q2 $113k) but 658 MW binding PPAs = $7.2B contracted backlog, 3 GW framework with Google, 2027 revenue guided $60-80M; Cape Station phase I (~100 MW) reported in commercial operation 30 Sep 2026 (sources conflict on timing). Revenue evidence weak, contracted backlog is the signal.

examples.company: Cerebras and Groq (Graphcore as the loser)
examples.evidence: Cerebras (2016) revenue $24.6M (2022), $290M (2024), $510M (2025); Q2 2026 GAAP revenue $180.1M (+74%), cloud/services +281% while hardware fell to $54.1M; RPO $25.4B at 30 Jun 2026; FY2026 core revenue guide $880-890M; IPO raised $5.55B; GAAP gross margin 14.2%; extreme concentration (G42+MBZUAI 86% of 2025 revenue per S-1 coverage; OpenAI, AWS also significant). Groq (2016) licensed to Nvidia for ~$20B (Dec 2025). Graphcore (2016) sold to SoftBank for ~$600M in 2024 after $2.7M 2022 sales vs $204.6M loss.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: The 2023-2026 AI buildout made power and inference speed the binding constraints for hyperscalers.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: My inference, not sourced: utilities and turbine makers could not deliver on-site power fast; GPU incumbents were not optimized for low-latency inference.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Open at the component/bottleneck level but capital-heavy and concentration-risky. Bloom's backlog is mostly cancelable service; Cerebras depends on a few buyers and has thin GAAP margin. Everything rides one industry's capex cycle.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: the payer is a hyperscaler with a named capex budget. Next bottlenecks behind power and chips: electrical gear and transformers, cooling, on-site construction labor, interconnection studies and permitting, water, optical/fiber links. Accessible small-team wedges are services/software around these (permitting, interconnection, commissioning, skilled-trade staffing for data-center builds). Verify with capex data in the pools stage.

patterns.name: A sovereign or infrastructure-capital backstop makes a capital-heavy, uninvestable industry bankable
patterns.mechanism: Strategic or capital-intensive industries die from price risk or cost of capital, not technology. A price floor, offtake, equity stake or standardized financing structure turns the business into a financeable contract and the customer's capex into a service fee.

examples.evidence: Jul 2025 DoD deal: $400M preferred stock (~15%, largest shareholder), 10-year NdPr price floor of $110/kg (China benchmark ~$63/kg at signing; DoD pays the difference), 10-year offtake on the new magnet plant. Q2 2026: revenue $108.5M (+89%) plus $17.6M price-protection income; NdPr sales 1,006 t (+127%); adj. EBITDA $28.5M. Molycorp's 2015 bankruptcy (predecessor) not verified in this run.

Brookfield's first AI-infrastructure investment, announced Oct 2025 at up to $5B, expanded to a $25B financing framework in Jun 2026 for onsite data-center power built with Bloom systems; customers get power as a service.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: US industrial policy for critical minerals (2025); infrastructure funds seeking AI exposure.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Pure-play commodity/equipment producers could not carry price risk against Chinese competition, and customers could not fund the capex (partly my inference).
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Open, but it rewards firms that can structure and operate, not idea founders; revenue so far modest (MP ~$108.5M a quarter).
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: where a government or large financier is publicly writing floors, offtakes or financing frameworks (critical minerals processing and magnets, grid equipment, munitions, shipbuilding inputs). For a small team the accessible layer is origination: underwriting, project data, servicing and insurance between equipment makers and infrastructure capital, since capital providers have mandates but few good deal flows (inference). Check each program's budget and eligibility.

patterns.name: A closed buyer reforms its purchasing, and a product-first, self-funded vendor wins
patterns.mechanism: Defense and other closed procurement systems favored cost-plus incumbents. When the buyer changes the rules (commercial-first buying, flexible contract vehicles), a vendor that builds the product with its own money and sells it as a finished product can win contracts in months instead of years.

examples.evidence: $5B Series H at $61B (May 2026, Thrive, a16z); 2025 revenue ~$2.1-2.2B, roughly double the prior year (secondary sources conflict on earlier years); ~27.7x revenue vs ~1.6-2.7x for prime contractors; DIU put it under contract for Replicator autonomy software in 110 days.

Hegseth's Nov 2025 memo 'Transforming the Warfighting Acquisition System' favors OTAs and Commercial Solutions Openings over the FAR; DIU has awarded 500+ OTAs since 2016, 88% to non-traditional vendors. Startups still get <1% of Pentagon contract dollars (~$1.8B FY2023 to $4.3B FY2025, Bloomberg Mar 2026); PitchBook counts a record $16.8B of defense/aerospace startup investment in H1 2026.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Procurement reform (2025) plus wartime-pace demand signals; DIU/OTA groundwork since 2016.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Primes optimized for cost-plus programs and long timelines; earlier startups lacked a contract path (partly inference).
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Capital is flooding in (record H1 2026), so valuations are stretched and founders chase the same subsystems; the unserved edge is the supply-chain and operations layer behind the hardware. Startup share of spend is still ~1%, which means room but also proof that spending is slow to move.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: other closed buyers with a reform or new contract vehicle and a large budget: border and homeland-security technology, Coast Guard and shipbuilding, state/local public safety and emergency management, public transit and utilities procurement. Small-firm wedge: compliance, program capture and supplier services; verify which budgets are actually appropriated.

patterns.name: A consumer hardware form factor works when a category-owning incumbent supplies brand, channel and manufacturing
patterns.mechanism: New devices fail when they are ugly, expensive, short on battery and short on a reason to exist. The unlock was packaging a familiar object with just enough new function and shipping it through the incumbent that owns the category's brand and stores.

examples.evidence: More than 7M smart glasses sold in 2025 per EssilorLuxottica's Q4-2025 report (>3x 2024, ~2M cumulative 2023-24); capacity target 10M/yr by end 2026 with reported talks of 20M+; Omdia counted 8.7M AI glasses shipped worldwide in 2025; $799 Ray-Ban Display intl rollout delayed Jan 2026 by demand/supply limits. Revenue is booked by EssilorLuxottica and Meta, not a startup.

examples.company: Google Glass, Intel Vaunt, North Focals (the dead)
examples.evidence: Glass consumer version ended ~2015 (privacy backlash, $1,500, 3-5 hour battery, no clear use); Glass Enterprise sold until 15 Mar 2023; Intel Vaunt cancelled Apr 2018 (ex-head: model assumed free hardware, data-protection questions unanswered); North Focals (~$999, est. <1,000 units) bought by Google Jun 2020 for patents and staff.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Good-enough voice AI, camera and audio in a normal frame, and a fashion brand with retail reach (my synthesis; the sources give numbers and failures but do not themselves explain the success).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Tech firms built gadgets for early adopters; nobody with frames, fitting stores and brand was in the room.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Closed for startups on glasses (Meta and EssilorLuxottica hold the channel). Open as a template: tech plus a category owner.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES: categories with a dominant physical-retail brand and a clear sensing/AI addition (eyewear, hearing, fitness equipment, watches, dental and optical retail). A small company's route is to be the software/data partner to a category owner rather than shipping its own hardware.

patterns.name: Labor-line conversion: human-in-the-loop services that died on labor cost become outcome-priced software once language models exist
patterns.mechanism: Services that needed humans to finish the job lost money at scale. Language models cut the marginal cost of the human part, so a vendor can price per resolved outcome against the customer's existing labor or outsourcing budget, a large already-budgeted pool.

examples.evidence: $100M ARR announced ~21 months in (late 2025), ~$150M by early Feb 2026; $950M Series E at $15.8B (May 2026); pay-per-resolution pricing; customers include ADT, Cigna, SiriusXM, Rivian, SoFi. ~100x ARR valuation signals froth. Customer-service agents are in round 1's cliche zone; use only as proof of the mechanism.
Valued $4.5B in Jan 2026 (Coatue, Index) on ~$35M ARR in Oct 2025 (3x YoY); a later report of >$100M ARR is NOT confirmed by the company (TechCrunch: no revenue disclosed since late 2024).

examples.company: Facebook M (dead 2018); Olive AI as warning
examples.evidence: Facebook M shut 19 Jan 2018 after ~2.5 years, reached ~2,000 Californians, contractors answering around the clock (press reading: human labor vs AI capability); Magic pivoted to B2B human+AI staffing. Olive AI (raised ~$832-902M, $4B valuation) died in 2023 from lack of focus, so a hot automation thesis does not save an unfocused company.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: LLMs from late 2022 onward, plus outcome-based pricing as a business model.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: BPOs sell hours (automation cuts their revenue) and legacy contact-center software sells seats (partly inference).
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Customer service is crowded (Sierra, Decagon and others). Other labor lines are less crowded but need domain depth and regulatory handling.
patterns.transfer_targets: HYPOTHESES needing pool sizing: language-heavy, measurable-outcome, compliance-bounded back-office labor that is outsourced today and run by people on phones and documents: insurance first-notice-of-loss and claims intake, healthcare denial appeals and prior authorization (CMS API mandates give a deadline), freight brokerage carrier check-calls, property-management leasing and maintenance dispatch, collections and KYC operations. The signer is the head of operations who owns the outsourced contract.

patterns.name: ANTI-PATTERN: False dawn, where capital arrives before the paying customer
patterns.mechanism: A claimed unlock (new models, new hardware) produces huge rounds, but customers are still piloting and press treats pilots as demand. 'No revenue number' should sharply lower the score; many 'we were too early' stories are really product or economics failures.

examples.company: Humanoid robot startups (Figure, Agility, Apptronik, Unitree)
examples.evidence: Counterpoint: global humanoid sales revenue first exceeded $500M in 2025, top three firms ~56%, Unitree ~CNY 879M (~$129M) in first 9 months 2025. Figure's 11-month BMW deployment is called a pilot by other analysts; Agility put 7 Digits at Toyota Canada (Feb 2026) and moved 100,000+ totes at GXO; Apptronik's mature product targeted for 2027, 0 verified at-scale deployments per one research site. Sources are aggregators.

Closed 3 Oct 2018 after a buyer pulled out and sales fell short; analysts blamed product-market mismatch and precision complaints; CEO Eckert said 'We got out a little early.' Other non-early deaths verified in this run: Olive AI (lack of focus), Transatomic Power (overstated claims), Zume (two capital-heavy businesses in one), Kozmo/Webvan (no delivery density).

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Claimed: foundation models for manipulation; hard evidence of purchase orders is thin.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Not applicable; the question is whether anyone has paying volume yet.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Unknown; sector revenue is under $1B globally and mostly a Chinese seller, so treat as unproven.
patterns.transfer_targets: Use as a gate rule for round 2: an 'unlock' counts only if (1) there is a dated catalyst, (2) a named buyer already pays at scale for a close substitute, and (3) revenue reaches at least tens of millions within ~24 months of the catalyst. Score pilots, press releases, valuations and 'orders' as zero. Other warning signs seen: AST commercial service slipped to 2027 after an Apr 2026 launch failure, Part 108 two quarters late, Aurora $2M quarterly revenue vs $266M loss.

patterns.name: Mass-market digital bank that wins thin-file credit
patterns.mechanism: A zero-fee account is acquired at near-zero cost in a market where a few banks charge high fees and refuse thin-file customers. The account generates transaction data, credit cards, personal loans and payroll loans are underwritten on that data, and cheap deposits fund the book. Revolut's variant leads with FX/travel, then monetizes subscriptions, cards, interest and wealth.

examples.evidence: FY2025 revenue ~US$16.4B (+45%), net income ~US$2.9B (+51%), ROE ~30%; 131M customers (Brazil 113M = 62% of adults; Mexico 14M = 15%; Colombia 4.2M = 11%). Plans US$4.2B in Mexico by 2030; OCC conditional approval for a US national bank (Jan 2026). Grade B: NeoFeed summary, 20-F not opened.

2025 revenue ~EUR5.3B / US$6.0B (+46%), pre-tax profit ~US$2.3B, net profit ~US$1.7B, 68.3M retail customers; subscriptions ~US$936M (+67%); deposits ~US$67.5B; loan book ~US$2.9B (doubled). Grade A/B.

Full bank license; ~2.5M active credit customers and a US$563M loan book; valuation US$1.5B (Mar 2025) to US$3.1B (Oct 2025) to a reported ~US$5B (Apr 2026). NO revenue figure found, so this is investor belief, not revenue proof. Grade C.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Instant payment rails (Pix), regulator-granted non-bank licenses (Mexico's CNBV licenses, Brazil's institution licenses), smartphone penetration, and open-finance data. The licensing detail is partly prior knowledge; Plata's license is sourced.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference, not sourced: fee-rich branch banks serve a narrow formal-income base, score only on bureau history, and have no reason to cannibalize card and account fees. Cost to serve with branches is far above an app-only model.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Crowded, and the winners are going global. Nubank has conditional OCC approval for a US bank (Jan 2026); in Mexico Nu (14M customers), Plata, Klar and Mercado Pago are all funded. No gap found in the home markets.
patterns.transfer_targets: No untouched US segment found. The US mechanism is already ported (Chime, Cash App, SoFi, Dave; prior knowledge) and Nubank itself is arriving. The transfer is geographic: countries with concentrated banks and high card APRs, which is not an obvious US-founder wedge. Unverified hypothesis: ITIN or immigrant thin-file credit in the US.

patterns.name: Marketplace-owned payments and credit flywheel
patterns.mechanism: The marketplace owns logistics, payments and credit. Commerce data lets it underwrite buyers and merchants more cheaply than any bank, float funds the credit book, and free shipping drives purchase frequency. Owned logistics is the moat.

examples.evidence: Q4 2025 net revenue US$8.8B (+45%), FY revenue +39%; Mercado Pago Q4 revenue US$3.8B (+51%); credit portfolio US$12.5B (+90%), 15-90 day NPL 4.4%, ~78M MAU; margins compressed 5-6 points by free shipping and credit-card investment. Grade A/B.
Q2 2025 Rocket Delivery (Product Commerce) adj. EBITDA $663M, a 9% margin; Taiwan, Eats and Farfetch lose ~$235M a quarter. FY2025 revenue ~$34.5B is from an aggregator and unverified. Grade B.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Weak postal systems forced owned logistics, low card penetration pushed wallets and credit, and Pix cut payment costs (the Pix point is partly prior knowledge).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: store-led retailers were weak at logistics and at underwriting small merchants on sales data; banks did not lend against marketplace sales history.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Closed at national scale: the moat is logistics plus capital, with no room for a me-too. Open only in verticals.
patterns.transfer_targets: Not the horizontal version (Amazon is the US incumbent). The transferable idea is a vertical B2B marketplace where small buyers carry 30-90 day payables and the marketplace finances the gap. Unverified hypotheses: independent-restaurant supply, independent-pharmacy wholesale, auto-repair parts. Assume someone already does each (Faire, Toast Capital, Amazon Business, Sysco/US Foods, FBN; prior knowledge).

patterns.name: Control the repayment channel (payroll deduction or wallet sweep)
patterns.mechanism: The lender is repaid first, from payroll or wallet inflows, so losses and rates fall far below revolving credit. Borrowers refinance and volume explodes. The state or a telco builds the channel, and lenders compete on top of it.

examples.company: Brazil Crédito do Trabalhador (private payroll loans, launched 21 Mar 2025)
examples.evidence: R$101B lent, 17.04M contracts, 8.52M workers by 15 Jan 2026 (Ministry of Labor via Poder360). Average rate 3.2% a month, ~46% a year (my calc), versus ~11.2% a month on CDC/card revolver/overdraft (~258% a year, my calc). Monthly private payroll lending rose from ~R$1.5B to ~R$11B (Serasa/Central Bank); Banco do Brasil alone lent R$18.2B. Central Bank warns of indebtedness; no program default rate found. Grade A/B.

FY to Mar 2026: KSh1.47T disbursed (+49%), 17.7M customers, average loan KSh218 (down from 241). Reported revenue KSh6B is only 0.41% of disbursements (my calc), so treat it as net or partial and do not use it as a margin proof. Grade B/C.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: In Brazil the state built an employer-agnostic platform on its payroll data (prior knowledge: private payroll loans previously needed employer-by-employer agreements; the cited articles do not describe the design). In Kenya the shift was M-Pesa's wallet float plus partner-bank licenses.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Banks could not reach employees outside large corporate agreements, and sub-$5 loans do not cover a bank's cost to serve (inference).
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Brazil is already crowding (Banco do Brasil and others), average ticket is falling and credit-quality alarms are sounding. In the US the category is open but legally gated.
patterns.transfer_targets: Best mechanism found, hardest to port. The Brazilian breakout came from the state removing the distribution bottleneck, not from a product innovation, and the US has no equivalent rail. Nearest rail owners are payroll processors and large employers. Legal gate: CFPB Dec 2025 advisory opinion treats employer-offered payroll-settled no-recourse EWA as not credit; H.R. 9330 advanced 29-22 on 30 Jun 2026 and is not law; about a dozen state EWA laws, with CA/CT/MD treating EWA as credit. Installment loans repaid by payroll deduction (state small-loan and wage-deduction law) were NOT researched. No employer budget line exists, only a retention motive. US pool size not sourced. Fuliza-style auto-overdraft is already ported (Cash App Borrow, Chime MyPay, Dave, EarnIn).

patterns.name: Remote-lock collateral with mobile-money collections and local-currency securitization (PAYG)
patterns.mechanism: If the customer stops paying, the product stops working, and that lockout is the collateral. Daily micropayments flow through mobile money. Each customer cohort becomes an asset-backed security funded in local currency, avoiding FX mismatch.

examples.evidence: FY2025 revenue ~US$600M (+45%), 10M customers (3M added in 12 months), ~50,000 agents, products now smartphones (since 2020), solar and e-motorcycles. Company says it stayed profitable but gives no profit number; underwriting and funding sources undisclosed; unaudited. Grade B/C.

US$156M (KES20.1B) local-currency securitization structured by Citi with Stanbic, backed by 5 banks and 3 DFIs, following a US$130M deal in 2023; US$1.3B of solar loans to ~10M customers; payments from US$0.19 a day via mobile money. No revenue figure found. Grade A for the deal.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Mobile money ubiquity, cheap GSM lock modules, smartphones as a second product, and a Kenyan securitization market now willing to buy micro-loan cash flows.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: banks cannot underwrite no-history customers, and microfinance lenders absorb repossession costs.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Two scaled players in Africa. The securitization is the proof the cash flows are bankable. No evidence found of an open gap.
patterns.transfer_targets: Weak. US incumbents are lease-to-own and rent-to-own (Progressive, Katapult, Upbound; prior knowledge), and state lease and repossession law differs. Speculative targets only: e-bikes for delivery workers, laptops, prepaid phones. No evidence of a US-scale gap was found.

patterns.name: Merchant-terminal or cash-agent network as distribution and underwriting data
patterns.mechanism: Where payments are free or thin-margin, the terminal or agent relationship supplies cash-flow data, the right to sweep settlement to repay loans, and a base to cross-sell accounts, devices and insurance. The payment itself is not the product. Lesson: dominating the rail does not make money.

examples.evidence: ~NGN412T (~US$294B) of transactions in 2025 and ~800M a month (company data via TechCabal); disbursed over NGN1T to ~70,000 small businesses (company year-in-review); valued at US$1B+ (FT, Oct 2024); says it is profitable, with NO audited revenue. CBN reports system NPLs at ~7% in 2025. A '$600M ARR' figure from one review site is unverified and was excluded. Grade A/B for volume, C for revenue.

~45% of 24.5B monthly UPI transactions (Aug 2026). FY25 revenue from operations ~Rs7,115 cr (+40%) but statutory net loss ~Rs1,727 cr; it has never posted a statutory profit. Non-UPI (merchant payments and financial services) is ~42% of revenue. Grade B (DRHP via press).

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: UPI's zero merchant fee and its scale in India; in Nigeria a push to cashless payments (prior knowledge).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: Nigerian banks had poor POS uptime and focused on corporate clients.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Crowded in both home markets (OPay and PalmPay in Nigeria; Google Pay and Paytm in India). Already ported and saturated in the US (Square, Toast, Clover, Shopify, Stripe).
patterns.transfer_targets: Avoid as a US idea. Volume does not equal revenue, since the profit is in credit and software on top of the terminal. Only possible angle: cash-heavy US segments with no software layer, which I did not size or verify.

patterns.name: Dense dark-store quick commerce
patterns.mechanism: Small warehouses sit inside dense neighborhoods. Delivery labor is cheap, order frequency is high and ads help. Profit needs very high throughput per store: Zepto does ~2,140 orders a store a day against ~3,000 to break even.

examples.evidence: FY26 orders: Blinkit 916.6M (2,243 stores), Zepto 640.2M (1,139), Instamart 412.2M (1,143). Only Blinkit is adj-EBITDA positive (Rs37 cr Q4 FY26; Rs102 cr Q1 FY27); Zepto lost Rs1,248 cr and Instamart Rs858 cr in Q4 FY26. Densification shows diminishing returns. Grade A/B.

Getir shut US, UK and EU operations and cut 6,000+ jobs; Gorillas sold for ~$1.2B against a $3.1B valuation a year earlier; Flink exited France and was valued at ~$1B against a ~$5B peak; hubs profit only at ~500-1,000 orders a day. No 2025-26 updates found. Grade B.
FY2025 GMV US$9.5B (+28%), revenue US$3.9B, adj. EBITDA US$615M (6.5% of GMV), net income US$464M, reinvesting $100M+ in grocery. Grade A (company release).

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: UPI-based payments, very low rider cost and kirana (corner-store) substitution (the last is prior knowledge).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: kiranas cannot offer assortment and big grocers lack last-mile delivery.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: India is a three-way discount war (Blinkit ~45-49% share, estimates conflict). Europe is dead. Gulf is served by Talabat and others.
patterns.transfer_targets: Do not port to the US: labor cost and density kill the unit economics, as Getir and Gorillas showed in rich-world cities. Only the ad-monetization and private-label pieces transfer.

patterns.name: Flip which side pays the marketplace fee
patterns.mechanism: Charge the side that values protection or convenience (the buyer, via a protection fee), or charge supply a small flat subscription instead of a commission. Supply keeps its margin, floods in, and gives the marketplace liquidity.

examples.evidence: 2025 revenue EUR1.1B (+38%), GMV EUR10.8B (+47%), net profit EUR62M (-19% from EUR77M), FCF EUR137M, valuation EUR8B. Sellers pay no commission; buyers pay a protection fee (amounts are third-party estimates). Revenue/GMV ~10.2% (my calc). Launched in the US in January 2026 starting in New York with 'tens of millions' in marketing. Grade A/B.

FY25 operating revenue Rs934.4 cr (+44%; Inc42 says nearly 2x, a conflict), net loss Rs258.4 cr. Replaced a 20-25% commission with a flat Rs9-29 a day (~5% of ride income). Uber moved India autos to subscription on 18 Feb 2025. GST treatment of subscription platforms is disputed across rulings. Grade B.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Rapido: driver anger over commissions plus a tax-ruling gap in India. Vinted: European parcel-locker infrastructure and consumer-protection norms. Both are partly inference.
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Prior knowledge: eBay, Poshmark and Depop were built on seller fees of 10-20%, which suppresses supply and lowers prices.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Vinted is in the US now, so a US clone is closed, and its profit fell 19% while investing. Rapido is still loss-making, and a flat fee caps revenue per ride.
patterns.transfer_targets: Vinted's US launch is the live experiment (its CEO says next year's profit depends partly on it). Unverified hypothesis for other categories: supply-scarce service marketplaces where pros pay per lead, such as home-services lead generation, trades and per-diem healthcare staffing. The gate is contractor classification (AB5, Prop 22; prior knowledge, legal premise unverified).

patterns.name: Own the supply chain, win on price
patterns.mechanism: Own the factory, ingredients or logistics, price 30-50% below incumbents to win traffic, and make money on the supply layer rather than on royalties.

examples.company: Mixue (China-origin; big in Indonesia and Vietnam)
examples.evidence: 2025 revenue RMB33.56B (+35%), net profit ~RMB5.93B, 59,823 stores. ~98% of revenue is goods and equipment sold to franchisees (RMB32.77B); franchise fees only RMB794M (2.4%); goods gross margin slipped to 29.9% from 31.2%. Overseas stores FELL from 4,895 to 4,467 as it optimized Indonesia and Vietnam while entering the US. Grade A/B.

FY25 operating revenue Rs6,652.5 cr (+22.5%), EBITDA ~Rs971 cr, 2,806 stores, claims 35-40% lower frame and lens cost from in-house automated manufacturing. Net profit Rs297 cr includes a ~Rs167 cr one-off gain, so operating profit is closer to Rs130 cr. Grade B.
FY2025 revenue ~VND157.4T (~US$6B, +16%), profit ~VND7.1T (~US$273M); its grocery chain took eight years (to Dec 2023) to break even. Grade B.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Manufacturing scale and automation (prior knowledge).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: fragmented independents lack purchasing scale, and incumbents sell on brand premiums.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Supply-margin franchising is old in the US (Domino's; prior knowledge). Mixue's own overseas retreat shows the price point does not survive higher local costs. Vertical-integration incumbents exist (EssilorLuxottica, Warby Parker, Zenni; prior knowledge).
patterns.transfer_targets: Weak. The price-point arbitrage fails on US labor and rent. What transfers is the screening question: find categories where the US retail layer is the cost, then own the supply chain behind it. Candidate categories (eyewear, hearing aids) already have incumbents, and none were sized here.

patterns.name: Instant-pay spot-labor marketplace in a shortage economy
patterns.mechanism: Remove the friction of staffing (no interview, no contract, short shifts, instant pay) so idle labor becomes just-in-time capacity for employers that cannot hire.

examples.evidence: FY to Oct 2025 revenue JPY34.28B (+27.5%) on GTV JPY117.2B, ~29% take rate (my calc). Registered workers 12.74M (Oct 2025) to 14.2M+ (Apr 2026), client sites 417k to 465k (aggregator-sourced). Latest quarter revenue JPY10.44B (+24.8%), operating profit JPY1.94B, but spot-work growth slowed to +16.3%. Fiscal-year change makes comparisons messy. Grade B.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Japan's labor shortage and side-job liberalization (prior knowledge).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: dispatch staffing required contracts, lead time and minimum durations.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Crowded in the US (Instawork, Wonolo, ShiftKey, Clipboard Health, Snagajob; prior knowledge), and Timee's own growth is decelerating.
patterns.transfer_targets: Low. Gates are W-2 versus 1099 classification, state staffing law and workers' comp. Per-diem nursing is the biggest sub-pool and already contested. No clearly untouched US pool found.

patterns.name: Mandate-created compliance rails
patterns.mechanism: A regulator mandates structured B2B invoice exchange through certified intermediaries. Every VAT-registered company must buy, on a legal deadline, and revenue is recurring per document or per seat. Accountants are the distribution channel. The payer (CFO or tax director) has a forced budget line.

examples.company: EU e-invoicing mandates (Belgium, Poland, France, Germany)
examples.evidence: Belgium live 1 Jan 2026 (Peppol); Poland KSeF 1 Feb 2026 (large) and 1 Apr 2026 (rest), micro-firms 2027; France from 1 Sep 2026 (large and mid issue, all must receive, SMEs 1 Sep 2027) via certified PDP platforms plus e-reporting; Germany receive 2025, send 2027; EU ViDA framework by 2030. Grade B; confirm France against the tax authority.
Acquired for ~US$800M (SEK8.1B), closed 26 Feb 2024 after beating a rival bid from Vertex; network of 90,000 customers reaching 14M companies, compliant with mandates in 75+ countries. Grade A/B.

EUR2B valuation (Apr 2025); claimed to exceed EUR100M ARR in 2025 (company claim); ~4,500 accounting firms and 350k SMEs; claims certified PDP status. A $4.25B round was reported in talks and is unconfirmed. Grade C for revenue.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Governments closing VAT gaps through real-time reporting, now an EU-wide program (prior knowledge for the motive; the mandate dates are sourced).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Mostly they did not fail: Pagero, Sovos, Avalara and Basware are the incumbents. ERPs were simply not built for real-time tax reporting, which created the opening for new certified platforms.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Consolidating fast at the enterprise tier (Thomson Reuters/Pagero, Vertex's bid). The SME tier still has years of mandate calendar (France SMEs 2027, Germany send-side 2027-28). No reliable revenue found for Sovos, Avalara or Basware.
patterns.transfer_targets: There is no US VAT or e-invoicing mandate, so a direct port has no mandated spend. The mechanism ports to US rules that force data exchange. Unverified hypotheses from prior knowledge, with every date to be checked: CMS prior-authorization API rule (CMS-0057-F), FDA DSCSA drug serialization, and FSMA 204 food traceability (deadline extended to 2028). Round 1 died on why-now windows that expired or arrived after 2028, so check deadlines first.

patterns.name: Stablecoin and alternative rails for FX-constrained corridors
patterns.mechanism: Stablecoin settlement plus a licensed local off-ramp replaces correspondent banking. Value is captured through FX spread and float, and the fee pool compresses as volume moves onto the new rail.

examples.evidence: ~US$6.5B of US-to-Mexico remittances in 2024, over 10% of the corridor (Bitso's own statement via Paymentology); corridor US$64.7B (BBVA Research), 96.6% from the US. June 2025 launched USD accounts for Mexico and Argentina (ACH US$2.99; wire US$11.99 + 0.17%). A '14.7% share in 2026' LinkedIn claim is unverified and excluded. Grade B/C.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: FX-access limits in Mexico and Argentina (per Bitso executives). On the US side the GENIUS Act, signed July 2025, is NOT yet effective: it takes effect by 18 Jan 2027 at the latest, and final rules were still pending in Aug 2026 (OCC targets November).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: money transmitters are slow and fee-heavy, with correspondent banking costs baked in.
patterns.still_open_or_crowded: Crowded with Remitly, Wise, Western Union, Circle and Coinbase (prior knowledge). The pool is large but price-compressing.
patterns.transfer_targets: $100M test, my arithmetic: if sender cost is 2-4% of the US$64.7B Mexico corridor (my assumption, not sourced), the fee pool is ~US$1.3-2.6B a year, so US$100M of revenue needs roughly 4-8% of it. US rules landing in 2027 give a timing edge to anyone building the US-side license stack. Prior knowledge to verify: a 1% US excise tax on cash-funded remittances began 1 Jan 2026, pushing senders to account-funded rails.

patterns.name: Curated retail and fast brand incubation, exported to the US
patterns.mechanism: A hyper-competitive home retail market (Olive Young's curation and rotation) works as a fast feedback loop. Surviving brands export through TikTok, Amazon and Sephora to US buyers who pay higher prices.

examples.evidence: Record US$11.43B of exports in 2025 (+12.3%); the US overtook China as the top destination (~US$2.2B vs ~US$2.0B). H1 2026 exports ~US$7B (+27%) with the US at ~US$1.45B (20.7%), though customs and MFDS series differ. Grade A/B for the macro numbers.

Over half of its global online sales came from US consumers in H1 2025; opened a Pasadena store and is placing Olive Young zones in Sephora. NO company revenue figures found for Olive Young or APR/Medicube. Grade C for companies.

patterns.shift_that_enabled_it: Social commerce and Amazon fulfillment (prior knowledge).
patterns.why_incumbents_failed: Inference: US prestige beauty iterates on slow cycles while Korean contract manufacturers move fast.

pools.name: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
pools.size_basis: About $15B of IDR payouts in 2025, more than triple 2024's $4.08B, per a WSJ analysis of CMS data (read via Healthcare Dive). Georgetown/Health Affairs estimates cumulative cost 2022-25 at $22.4B ($15.6B above-benchmark payments, $4.2B admin, $2.7B arbiter fees), which I only saw second-hand. Volume ~1.2M disputes H1 2025 and ~1.4M H2 2025 vs 17,000/yr expected by government.
pools.money_flow: Plans and self-funded employers (via TPAs) pay out-of-network emergency, radiology, anesthesia and hospital-based physicians the offer an arbiter picks, plus a $115 admin fee per party and arbiter fees. Providers and billing intermediaries start ~99.9% of disputes; providers win ~85% with median award ~445% of the plan's in-network benchmark (QPA).
pools.shock: En banc Fifth Circuit (TMA III, 2026-08-11) held the federal QPA rules unlawful on 'ghost rates' and excluded bonus/risk-share payments, so every payer's benchmark methodology is defective and past QPAs may need recomputation; agencies also finalized an IDR Operations Rule in May 2026; insurers are lobbying Congress to overhaul IDR while volume keeps rising 16% half over half.
pools.incumbents: Provider side: PE-backed physician groups (Team Health, SCP Health, Radiology Partners) and contingency billing intermediary HaloMD (~56% of H1 2025 disputes among the top four). Payer side: Claritev (ex-MultiPlan), Zelis, Cotiviti, Fair Health benchmarks, big-carrier in-house teams (UnitedHealthcare, BCBS Texas, Aetna are 57% of disputes).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Payers lose ~85% of disputes and, per physician-group analysis of CMS data, default on roughly 1 in 4 line items; self-funded employers who ultimately fund awards have no defense tooling; the QPA, the legal anchor of the system, was just ruled defective; arbiters are throughput-constrained. Risk: Congress could cap awards and shrink the pool.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Daffodil Health (payer-side OON pricing/payment integrity, $16.3-16.6M Series A, Flare Capital, ~$20.9M total, 2025-26); Radix Health (software IDR, provider side); Pivotal Health (provider-side IDR, success fee); HaloMD has no disclosed funding I could find. None found for TPA/self-funded-employer IDR defense.
pools.wedge_hints: (a) IDR defense and default-prevention for hundreds of mid-size payers and TPAs with no in-house team; (b) QPA recomputation/audit service after TMA III; (c) pre-IDR negotiation and OON carve-outs for self-funded employers; (d) software for the arbitration entities themselves.
pools.insider_roles: Payer OON/NSA compliance directors, TPA claims-operations VPs, ED and radiology group revenue-cycle directors, IDR-entity reviewers, benefits attorneys.

pools.name: State Medicaid program administration, esp. the H.R.1 work-requirement and six-month-renewal build-out
pools.geography: US (41 expansion jurisdictions for work requirements)
pools.size_basis: State program administration was $41,325M in FY2024 ($25.3B federal, $16.0B state) of $957B total Medicaid (MACPAC Exhibit 16, read). The shock-affected slice is far smaller: CMS estimates ~$15M average systems cost per state ($660M nationally) excluding ongoing verification, notices and appeals; AP counted >$1B across 25+ states; federal implementation grant is only $200M.
pools.money_flow: States (federal match 90% system build, 75% operations, 50% general admin) pay IT integrators, eligibility vendors, call centers, enrollment brokers and data brokers; Medicaid managed-care plans separately pay for member outreach and retention because each disenrollment loses premium revenue.
pools.shock: H.R.1 requires 80 hours/month of work, service or education for expansion adults 19-64 from 2027-01-01 plus six-month redeterminations; CMS issued the interim final rule 2026-06-01 (effective 2026-07-31), projecting ~2.3M fewer enrollees in FY2027; good-faith exemptions expire by 2028-12-31.
pools.incumbents: Deloitte, Gainwell, Maximus, Accenture, Conduent, GDIT, Optum, Acentra, Merative (Curam), RedMane (pledged $600M+ of free/discounted services in Jan 2026); Equifax Work Number (used by ~half of states per Warren/Wyden/Sanders letter).
pools.incumbent_fragility: State eligibility systems are patchworks never built to pull and track data from many sources; integrators are discounting under White House pressure; the employment-data layer is a near-monopoly under political fire; Arkansas's earlier trial dis-enrolled people for paperwork failure, so errors carry legal risk. Buyer is state procurement (slow); $100M needs ~20 states at ~$5M or per-verification pricing across millions of people.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found specifically for Medicaid work-requirement verification (searched Nava, Propel, Benefit Kitchen, Truss, Gridwise, Truv, Argyle, Pinwheel; no relevant 2026 hits). Field is dominated by giant integrators giving services away.
pools.wedge_hints: (a) Alternative income/employment verification (payroll APIs, state UI wage records, gig platforms) priced per verification; (b) plan-paid member documentation and retention outreach; (c) volunteer/community-service hour verification; (d) medical-frailty exemption documentation for FQHCs and providers.
pools.insider_roles: State Medicaid eligibility directors and MMIS project managers, managed-care government-programs VPs, county eligibility workers, FQHC enrollment staff, legal-aid attorneys.

pools.name: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
pools.size_basis: HRSA reports covered entities bought $100B of outpatient drugs in CY2025, up ~22% from $81.4B in CY2024; hospitals ~87%. The contestable money (spread, administration, compliance) is a fraction and I could not source it.
pools.money_flow: Manufacturers sell outpatient drugs at statutory ceiling prices to ~50,000 covered-entity sites; entities bill Medicare and insurers at full rates and keep the spread, increasingly via contract pharmacies run by third-party administrators.
pools.shock: First HRSA rebate pilot was enjoined (D. Maine 2025-12-29) and withdrawn Feb 2026; D.C. Circuit (Novartis v. Kennedy, 2026-07-21) held rebate models lawful only with HHS approval; HRSA published a revised pilot 2026-08-03 effective 2027-01-01 (pay full price, submit claims data, get rebate); AHA sued again 2026-10-09; Congress has competing drafts (Cassidy draft allows rebates or a claims repository, House SECURE 340B Act pauses rebates, Senate SUSTAIN 340B Act moves to a data clearinghouse).
pools.incumbents: Third-party administrators and contract-pharmacy networks (Sentry/Wellpartner, Walgreens, CVS, Verity, Second Sight's 340B ESP) and Kalderos (duplicate-discount and rebate platform).
pools.incumbent_fragility: A rebate model forces hospitals and safety-net clinics to front full price and prove claims-level eligibility: a working-capital and data problem for thin balance sheets and weak data teams. The data standard (clearinghouse vs manufacturer platforms) is unresolved. Risk: outcome splits three ways (rebates, discounts-with-data, pause) and depends on courts and Congress within ~12 months.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Proximity ($3M seed, Feb 2025, LRVHealth/Commonweal; 340B revenue automation); Pillr Health (Water Street Healthcare Partners investment Jan 2026, size undisclosed; split billing, contract pharmacy, rebate readiness); Kalderos ($7M Series A 2019, $28M Series B 2020, Bain Capital Ventures; no 2023-26 round found).
pools.wedge_hints: Advance financing against 340B rebate receivables; claims-data scrubbing and rebate-submission service for small covered entities and FQHCs; duplicate-discount prevention; a neutral claims clearinghouse if Congress picks that model.
pools.insider_roles: 340B program directors at DSH hospitals and FQHCs, hospital pharmacy directors, manufacturer 340B-integrity leads, TPA compliance staff, health-system treasurers.

pools.name: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
pools.size_basis: CMS: 7.8M HCBS users and $129.4B of Medicaid spending in 2022 (+12.5% y/y); narrower personal-care slice ~$46.4B in 2024 (nearly double 2019) per RealClearInvestigations, New York alone $15.67B.
pools.money_flow: State Medicaid agencies (and managed-LTSS plans) pay thousands of small home care agencies and fiscal-intermediary payroll firms per care hour; most revenue passes through as aide wages.
pools.shock: H.R.1 cuts federal Medicaid by $911B over 2025-34 (KFF), and states historically cut HCBS enrollment and rates; immigration enforcement hits a workforce that is >40% foreign-born for home health aides; New York consolidated ~600 fiscal intermediaries into one statewide FI (PPL) on 2025-04-01 for ~250k consumers; the 80/20 wage pass-through rule (effective ~2030) remains unrescinded.
pools.incumbents: Fiscal intermediaries (PPL, GT Independence, Acumen/Tempus), agency chains (Addus, BrightSpring, Amedisys), software (HHAeXchange for EVV, WellSky, AlayaCare, AxisCare, Axxess, ClearCare).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Thousands of agencies under $20M revenue on thin margins, paid late by states, squeezed by rate cuts and a shrinking labor supply, with EVV compliance burdens and no access to working capital; states are willing to restructure the whole market (New York).
pools.funded_startups_already_here: AlayaCare (C$225M Series D 2021; debt financing Feb 2026), Enzo Health ($20M Series A May 2026, home health/post-acute AI), MochaCare (~$1M accelerator round Mar 2026). No venture-funded Medicaid FI/payroll challenger found.
pools.wedge_hints: Working-capital advances against Medicaid receivables (balance-sheet business); fiscal-intermediary/payroll platform for states that bid statewide FIs after New York; EVV-to-claims reconciliation; caregiver pipeline products for agencies.
pools.insider_roles: Agency owners and administrators, state long-term-care program managers, FI operations VPs, EVV compliance leads, waiver case managers.

pools.name: Clinical laboratory testing (independent, hospital-outreach and reference labs)
pools.size_basis: US clinical lab services ~$99.7B revenue in 2024, projected $122.5B by 2029 (Hyde Park Capital, secondary). Medicare Part B lab spend $8.4B in 2024 per HHS OIG as cited by MarkNtel (secondary), 43% genetic tests. Narrow ~$10B market-research figures are not comparable.
pools.money_flow: Medicare, Medicare Advantage, commercial plans and Medicaid pay labs per test; Medicare's rate is set from a private-payer rate survey under PAMA, so Medicare cuts propagate to billing and contracting.
pools.shock: CMS's preliminary 2027 clinical lab fee schedule (week of 2026-09-25) applies the maximum 15% cut to ~775 tests (~1,200 tests total per ACLA) with more cuts in 2028-29, after Congress delayed cuts a seventh time in the Feb 2026 appropriations act; CMS says it saves ~$1B a year; the RESULTS Act (claims-database rate setting) is pending and analysts expect another delay.
pools.incumbents: Quest and Labcorp (buying hospital outreach labs), thousands of regional and specialty/genetic labs; billing systems XIFIN, Sunquest, Orchard, offshore RCM shops.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Independent labs run thin margins, depend on payer coverage decisions (MolDX) and the PAMA rate, and hospitals are selling outreach labs; billing is legacy or offshore. Risk: Congress may delay cuts again, weakening urgency.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found that are lab-specific revenue-cycle companies (general RCM adjacent: Candid Health $120M Series D, Silna Health $27M). Only three searches; low confidence.
pools.wedge_hints: Lab-specific underpayment and denial recovery on contingency; payer-rate benchmarking for labs in the 2025 PAMA data cycle; outreach-lab transition services for health systems.
pools.insider_roles: Independent-lab CFOs and billing managers, hospital outreach-lab directors, MolDX/coverage consultants, lab sales managers.

pools.name: Rural Health Transformation Program state grants
pools.size_basis: $10B a year for FY2026-FY2030 ($50B total) under H.R.1; FY2026 awards range $147M (NJ) to $281M (TX), avg ~$200M. Funding-notice limits (via Texas DSHS summary and AHA letter): provider payments capped at 15%, infrastructure 20%, EHR 5%, so roughly 60%+ goes to programs, technology, workforce and care-model pilots.
pools.money_flow: CMS to 50 states (half split equally, half by CMS-scored plans), then to state agencies, providers, vendors and workforce programs.
pools.shock: CMS announced first-year awards 2025-12-29; states must obligate year-one funds within ~10 months and spend within one more year or face claw-back and redistribution, with RFPs posting from July 2026 through Q1 2027; KFF frames it as an offset to Medicaid cuts.
pools.incumbents: State agencies, large consultancies (Deloitte, Guidehouse, Accenture), EHR vendors, telehealth vendors, rural hospital associations.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Spend-fast pressure creates many isolated pilots; no standard vendor for outcome tracking and subgrant management; rural hospitals lack grant-writing and IT capacity (AHA asking for technical-assistance centers). Risk: five-year grant then a cliff; vendor-addressable share is not public; slow state procurement.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found aimed at this program (searches returned only advisory and vendor-blog content).
pools.wedge_hints: Grant-management, compliance and outcome-reporting platform sold to 50 state RHT offices; subgrant application help for critical-access hospitals; shared IT/cyber/revenue-cycle services paid from program funds.
pools.insider_roles: State RHT program directors, rural hospital CFOs and CEOs, state hospital association staff, rural health clinic managers.

pools.name: Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment (coding-intensity) payments
pools.size_basis: MedPAC March 2026: Medicare pays ~14% more for MA enrollees than for the same people in fee-for-service, a projected $76B in 2026, from favorable selection (~11 points) and coding intensity (~4 points); MA plans were paid ~$537B in 2025. Coding slice ~4 points of ~$540B = ~$22B (my arithmetic, consistent with an outside analysis). Vendor spend on risk adjustment is not publicly sized.
pools.money_flow: CMS pays MA plans risk-adjusted capitation; plans spend on chart review, coding vendors, in-home assessments and encounter capture, and pay value-based provider groups.
pools.shock: CY2027 final rate notice (2026-04-06) gives +2.48% base but excludes diagnoses from unlinked chart reviews (CMS-estimated -1.53%) and audio-only encounters and keeps the 2024 model; RADV extrapolation rule was vacated 2025-09-25 and the Fifth Circuit heard the appeal ~2026-10-05, panel reportedly leaning to affirm.
pools.incumbents: Optum, Cotiviti, Episource, Inovalon, Lumeris, plan in-house teams.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Retrospective unlinked chart review, the core of the vendor business, is being excluded from payment; in-home assessment vendors face DOJ scrutiny; RADV enforcement is legally unstable. Strong incumbents and abundant startups limit openings.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: RAAPID (Series A extension Mar 2026 from UPMC Enterprises; earlier M12 and CareFirst's Healthworx); Keebler Health ($6M seed, $7.8M total, date unclear); list is partial.
pools.wedge_hints: Encounter-linked prospective documentation at the point of care; RADV defense and record retrieval for plans; compliance tooling for value-based groups.
pools.insider_roles: MA risk-adjustment directors, value-based group CMOs and coding managers, RADV appeals attorneys, certified coders.

pools.name: Hospital and post-acute claim denials, including Medicare Advantage prior-authorization denials
pools.size_basis: Premier survey of 516 hospitals (claims from 2022): hospitals spend ~$19.7B a year fighting denied claims (15% of private-payer claims denied, 54.3% eventually overturned, $43.84 per denial). Unverified secondary figures: AHA $43B spent on payer collections in 2025 incl. ~$18B on denials; vendor claim of $26B.
pools.money_flow: Providers spend labor and vendor fees to appeal payer denials; the money at stake is revenue recovered (skilled-nursing and hospital revenue from MA and commercial plans).
pools.shock: HHS OIG report OEI-09-24-00331 (2026-06-08): 19 MA parents denied 12% of skilled-nursing admission requests, 18% were appealed and 95% of appeals overturned; naviHealth (UnitedHealth) denied 14%; nursing-home residents denied 40%; Senate HSGAC letters to Humana, UnitedHealth, CVS on 2026-07-14.
pools.incumbents: R1 RCM, Waystar, Optum, Ensemble, Cotiviti; payers' automated utilization-management tools.
pools.incumbent_fragility: A 95% overturn rate on appeal means initial denials are a volume game, and providers under-appeal (11-18%); payer denial systems now face political scrutiny. But hospital denials are heavily funded and crowded.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Amperos Health ($16M Series A Apr 2026, Bessemer); Candid Health ($120M Series D, Sixth Street); RapidClaims ($11M, Accel); Basalt Health ($20M Series A, NEA, post-acute); ExaCare AI ($30M Series A, Insight, SNF referrals); Willow (YC, long-term-care RCM); Clinware ($4.25M seed); Cascala ($8.6M seed); R1 bought Humata Health.
pools.wedge_hints: Contingency appeals for skilled-nursing and home-health operators against MA denials (95% overturn rate gives a high win rate); payer-contract compliance audit for long-term-care operators.
pools.insider_roles: Hospital denial-management directors, SNF administrators and business-office managers, MA appeals nurses, payer medical directors.

pools.name: US homeowners insurance premiums in wildfire-, hail- and hurricane-exposed markets (California cat-model reform, Florida reinsurance reset)
pools.geography: US, concentrated in CA, FL, TX, CO, LA
pools.size_basis: S&P Global Market Intelligence on NAIC data: about $173.1B direct homeowners premium written in 2024 (+13.4%, combined ratio 99.3%); NAIC says 2025 growth slowed, so 173 is a floor. State Farm held about 19.4% of 2024 premium. Figure came via search summary of the S&P article, not read in full.
pools.money_flow: Households (via mortgage escrow) pay carriers and residual plans (CA FAIR Plan, FL Citizens). Carriers pay claims, cat reinsurers, agent commissions and modelers. Residual plans assess the industry when they lose money.
pools.shock: California Sustainable Insurance Strategy lets insurers price with forward-looking wildfire cat models and pass California-only reinsurance costs into rates in exchange for writing in distressed areas (85% of market share). CDI approved the Verisk wildfire model 2025-07-24; Mercury filed the first rate case by 2025-08-15. CDI's Aug 2026 brief: twelve insurer groups have filed under SIS, FAIR Plan growth under 2% in Q2 2026. FAIR Plan has about 668k policies and a roughly 30-35% rate hike for renewals from 2026-10-15 (secondary sources conflict). Opposite pole: Florida Citizens fell from about 1.4M policies (Sept 2023) to 293,772 (May 31, 2026) and June 2026 cat reinsurance fell 15-20%. NAIC: Palisades and Eaton were the costliest wildfires in world history.
pools.incumbents: State Farm, Allstate, Farmers, Progressive, USAA, Chubb, Mercury, CSAA; independent agents; cat modelers Verisk, Moody's RMS, KCC. Carriers earn the spread between premium and modeled loss; modelers license by seat.
pools.incumbent_fragility: State Farm General went to S&P CreditWatch Negative and sought an emergency 17% hike. California is prior-approval, so every change needs a filing and the regulator sets the pace. The 85% writing commitment must now be proven with data. Legacy policy and inspection workflows cannot ingest mitigation evidence at scale.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: RockRose Risk ($12.5M Series A, Aug 2026, vertically integrated wildfire mitigation plus insurance, plans to acquire tree-trimming and roofing firms); BurnBot (Mercury strategic investment, May 2026); BirdsEyeView (seven-figure round, Jan 2026, wildfire modeling); Zesty.ai (Series B 2022, CDI-accepted model, no 2026 round found); Kettle (wildfire reinsurance MGA, $25M Series A, older). From background knowledge, not re-verified: Kin, Openly, Hippo, Lemonade, Branch.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Verified-mitigation evidence layer: SIS forces discounts and published wildfire risk scores, but homeowners must prove work (photos, invoices, IBHS or third-party inspection; State Farm's 2024 version needed a $125 inspection fee) - a registry or inspection-and-repair network carriers accept. 2) FAIR Plan take-out tooling (policy matching, pricing, agent workflow) for the twelve SIS carriers; Florida's nine Citizens take-out approvals Feb-Apr 2026 are the template. 3) Wildfire rebuild and claims logistics (contractor capacity, permits) after Palisades and Eaton. 4) Parametric deductible top-ups sold through MGAs.
pools.insider_roles: CDI rate-filing analysts and carrier actuaries who file SIS cases; independent agents in California WUI zones; wildfire claims adjusters from Palisades/Eaton; FAIR Plan underwriters; Fire Safe Council and mitigation contractors; mortgage servicers' hazard-loss departments; Florida reinsurance brokers.

pools.name: Insurers' spend on property-catastrophe reinsurance and insurance-linked securities (cat bonds, collateralized re), now repricing down 12-25%
pools.geography: Global (US and Florida set the price)
pools.size_basis: WEAK BASIS, lower bound only. No sourced total of global property-cat reinsurance premium was found. Derived: ILS capital $144.5B at 6/30/2026 times a rate-on-line of about 8.5-12% (Florida Citizens' net ROL was 8.46% in 2026 and 11.95% in 2025) gives about $12-17B for third-party capital alone. Dedicated reinsurance capital is $648B (Gallagher Re, YE2025) to $790B (Aon, 3/31/2026), so the full premium pool including traditional reinsurers is several times larger but unquantified.
pools.money_flow: Primary insurers, state funds (Citizens, FHCF, CEA) and some corporates pay reinsurers and cat-bond investors for catastrophe limit. Brokers (Aon, Guy Carpenter, Gallagher Re, Howden) take brokerage; modelers sell the risk view.
pools.shock: January 1, 2026 renewals: Howden risk-adjusted property cat pricing -14.7% (largest drop since 2014), retro -16.5%; Guy Carpenter global property cat ROL index -12%, then -16% at mid-year, now 23% below the 2024 peak; Florida June 1 down 15-25%. Record $25.6B cat bonds issued in 2025, $63.4B outstanding mid-2026. Counter-signal: CDI's Aug 2026 brief warns cumulative losses point to higher reinsurance costs for 2027.
pools.incumbents: Munich Re, Swiss Re, Hannover Re, SCOR, Everest, Arch, RenaissanceRe; four large brokers; ILS managers. Reinsurers earn the spread over modeled loss; brokers earn a percentage of premium.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Only moderate. Falling rates shrink brokerage dollars while placement work stays manual (spreadsheets, bordereaux). A record capital glut means reinsurers chase large cedents and neglect the long tail of small insurers, public entities and corporates. Balance sheets are not fragile.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Kettle (wildfire reinsurance MGA, $25M Series A, older). Not verified: Reask, Oasis LMF, Fermat Capital and other cat-model and ILS tech names.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Repeatable small-ticket cat-bond or parametric shelf for regional insurers, municipalities and mid-size corporates (under about $50M limit) where reinsurer minimums bite. 2) Reinsurance procurement and bordereaux data tooling for the roughly 65 new E&S carriers and thousands of MGAs that each buy several treaties. 3) Collateral and trust accounting operations (LOCs, trusts). 4) Parametric top-ups attached to homeowners (Pool 1). Assume software or services to cedents, not capacity.
pools.insider_roles: Reinsurance brokers who place treaties; cedent reinsurance managers and CROs at regional carriers; cat modelers; ILS portfolio managers; trust and collateral administrators in Bermuda; parametric calculation agents.

pools.name: US commercial auto and trucking liability premiums
pools.size_basis: About $72.2B direct premium written in 2024 (+12.1%), AM Best as summarized in search results (not re-verified at source). NAIC 2025 report: commercial auto premium has risen for 15 straight years, +6.6% in Q4 2025 (highest of any line); commercial auto liability pure net loss ratio 71%.
pools.money_flow: Motor carriers and fleets pay carriers and MGAs, mostly through trucking-specialist agents. Carriers pay claims and defense counsel; verdicts above $10M ('nuclear') drive severity.
pools.shock: Two federal changes rewrite driver-qualification risk. English-language proficiency out-of-service enforcement began 2025-06-25 (DOT says 26,000+ drivers sidelined). The non-domiciled CDL final rule is effective 2026-03-16; FMCSA estimates 194,000 non-domiciled CDL holders affected. Commercial auto and GL are the only major lines still above 100% combined (Triple-I/Milliman, May 2026); S&P projects commercial auto at 104.4% in 2026 rising to 106.3% by 2029. The premium link from the new rules is mostly forecast so far; one executive said capacity has not yet fallen.
pools.incumbents: Progressive (among the largest trucking writers, background knowledge), Travelers, Liberty Mutual, Berkshire/National Indemnity, Old Republic, Sentry, Great West; specialty trucking agencies. They profit only if rate increases outrun severity, which they have not for years.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Roughly 15 years of underwriting pain; loss data and driver files sit in incompatible systems (telematics per fleet, MVR per state, FMCSA CSA scores); verdict inflation outruns filed rates; small-fleet agents cannot verify driver status. States regulate rates and the line is unprofitable, so carriers cut appetite rather than innovate.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Nirvana Insurance ($100M Series D at $1.5B valuation, over $260M raised, telematics, single-truck to 500+ truck fleets); Cover Whale (MGA, $40M from Morgan Stanley Expansion Capital Jul 2025, $1.3B+ GWP since 2020); LEEO (telematics commercial auto product launched Mar 2026); HDVI ($16M Series A, Munich Re Ventures and 8VC); Humn.ai ($13.7M Series A, UK, undated).
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Driver-qualification verification feed (CDL status, ELP out-of-service history, non-domiciled flags, chameleon-carrier detection) sold to carriers, MGAs and brokers as underwriting data, like MVR vendors. 2) Group captive or risk retention group formation for 20-100 truck fleets (see captive pool). 3) Post-crash evidence and rapid-response services to blunt nuclear verdicts, paid from carrier claims budgets.
pools.insider_roles: Trucking insurance agents at large specialty agencies; fleet safety directors; trucking claims adjusters and litigation managers at Progressive or Great West; defense counsel who try nuclear-verdict cases; FMCSA compliance consultants; loss-control engineers; CVSA inspectors.

pools.name: US workers' compensation system cost (medical, indemnity, claims administration, cost containment)
pools.size_basis: NASI (Aug 2026, 2023 data): $64.1B total benefits paid (medical plus cash) covering about 150M jobs. NCCI: private carriers wrote $41.6B net premium in 2025; the rest is state funds and self-insured employers. Total employer cost exceeds benefits (admin, profit, taxes) but is not sourced here.
pools.money_flow: Employers pay premiums (or self-insure) to carriers and state funds. Carriers and third-party administrators pay medical providers, injured workers and lawyers. Cost-containment vendors (bill review, PBMs, nurse case management) are paid per bill or as a share of savings.
pools.shock: NCCI State of the Line 2026 (May 2026): private carrier premium fell 0.2% in 2025, the only major line to shrink; calendar-year combined ratio rose to 91% from 86%; accident-year 2025 combined ratio is 102%, so profit now depends on old-reserve releases; medical claim severity rose 6% (2024 data).
pools.incumbents: Travelers, Hartford, Liberty, Zurich, Chubb, AmTrust; state funds (e.g., California SCIF); TPAs (Sedgwick, Gallagher Bassett, CorVel); medical cost containment (Enlyte, MedRisk, Healthesystems). Money is made on float, reserve releases and per-bill vendor fees.
pools.incumbent_fragility: 50 different fee schedules force national vendors to rebuild logic per state; savings-based vendor fees reward inflated 'savings'; premium audits and class-code disputes irritate the paying employer; reserve-release earnings are shrinking. Boring and fragmented rather than weak.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: CompScience ($27.6M Series B, Feb 2025, safety video analytics plus MGA); Pie Insurance (over $615M raised, Series D 2021); Hourly ($27M Series A, undated); Insurate (2021 seed). No 2026 rounds found for workers' comp claims, medical or nurse case-management startups.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Employer-side premium audit and class-code correction on contingency (employers have a premium line and hate audit disputes). 2) Medical bill-review exceptions and pharmacy cost transparency for self-insured employers and TPAs. 3) Return-to-work and case-management coordination networks. Check state anti-kickback and percent-of-savings rules.
pools.insider_roles: Workers' comp claims adjusters and nurse case managers; employer risk managers; applicant and defense attorneys; TPA operations heads; premium auditors; NCCI/WCIRB classification specialists; state fund underwriters.

pools.name: US title insurance premiums (money mostly retained by title agents)
pools.size_basis: NAIC 2025 full-year report (read as PDF): title direct premium written $18.6B in 2025 (+13.5%); ALTA says $18.5B (+13.8%). Settlement and escrow fees paid by buyers sit on top and are not counted. Non-affiliated agents handle 62.7% of premium; 72.6% of operating expenses are paid to or retained by agents.
pools.money_flow: Buyers and refinancing borrowers pay a one-time premium at closing. Agents keep most of it, underwriters keep the rest and pay claims. Net loss ratio is only 4.4% and expense ratio 98.5% (combined 102.8%, third straight year above 100%); paid losses and expense average $51 per policy.
pools.shock: FHFA/Fannie Mae title waiver pilot: Doma Title first vendor from Nov 2024, Westcor added Jul 2025; lenders can skip lender's title insurance on low-risk refinances and pay Fannie a $75 fee. In June 2026 FHFA director Pulte said Fannie was working to expand the pilot; KBW analysts called the earnings impact small and it is still refinance-only. Separately, 2025 premium jumped as refis revived when rates fell to about 6.5% in Sept 2025. ALTA argues fraud and forgery are about 40% of refi claim costs. Shock is real but small so far.
pools.incumbents: First American 23.1%, Fidelity National 14.5%, Old Republic 14%, Chicago Title 13.1%, Stewart 10.9% (ALTA via Scotsman Guide; top five over 75%); thousands of agencies; county recorders and local title plants as data gatekeepers.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Nearly all revenue is a one-time toll on a transaction while claims are 4.4% of premium, so the product is priced like distribution, not insurance. A federal buyer (Fannie/Freddie) can waive the requirement for loans it owns. But state statutes, the purchase-loan lender requirement and ALTA lobbying slow any bypass.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Qualia (closing platform; reported $50M round Aug 2026, sources conflict on series and valuation); Doma (first waiver vendor); Westcor (traditional underwriter, second waiver vendor); Spruce, States Title, JetClosing, Modus, Endpoint (named by Bain Capital Ventures, no 2026 rounds found); Blueprint Title ($16M Series B, 2021); Vestris (YC, end-to-end title processing).
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Automated title-risk product for the GSE waiver (needs a licensed underwriter partner; the $75 flat fee versus 4.4% loss ratio shows the margin is in not paying agents). 2) Wire-fraud and forgery prevention at closing (identity, wire verification). 3) National standardized title-plant and recorder data across 3,000+ counties licensed to underwriters, lenders and GSEs. 4) Commercial real estate title review as volumes rebound.
pools.insider_roles: Title examiners and underwriting counsel; escrow officers; title agency owners; county recorders; mortgage closers and post-closers; GSE seller/servicer relationship managers.

pools.name: US annuity and life insurance distribution compensation (agent commissions and IMO/FMO overrides)
pools.size_basis: DERIVED. LIMRA: 2025 annuity sales $461.3B (+6%), of which FIA $128.2B, RILA $79.6B, other about $253.5B. Assumed commissions (not verified at source; only Wink's 2017 average indexed-annuity commission of 4.96% found): FIA about 5% ($6.4B), RILA about 3.5% ($2.8B), other about 2.5% ($6.3B), total about $15.5B. A 3-5% blended range gives $14-23B. Life insurance commissions are extra and not counted.
pools.money_flow: Carriers (Athene, Corebridge, Allianz Life, Jackson, MassMutual, F&G) pay commissions to independent agents, banks and broker-dealers, plus overrides to IMOs/FMOs. Consumers pay through spread and surrender charges.
pools.shock: Record demand and a product mix shift: Q2 2026 was a record quarter at $123.9B and H1 2026 reached $231.3B (LIMRA); RILA +21%, FIA -5% as caps fell, fixed-rate deferred -7%. Mix shifts move commission dollars between channels. Hypothesis, unverified: surrender periods on 2022-2024 purchases are starting to end, creating a retention and rollover wave.
pools.incumbents: IMOs and FMOs (e.g., Integrity, AmeriLife - background knowledge), independent broker-dealers (LPL, Osaic), banks, career agencies, carrier wholesalers. Money is earned as override percentages and carrier bonuses.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Each carrier has its own application, illustration, suitability form and contracting process; best-interest rules add documentation burden; commissions compress as sales shift to lower-commission RILAs; overrides pay for manual back-office work. Lock-in is real though, since agents follow their IMO.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Ethos (term life, IPO Jan 2026 raising about $200M); DPL Financial Partners ($23M Series C, Dec 2024, RIA insurance marketplace); Annuity.com ($15.7M seed, May 2024); Axonic Insurance ($210M, Oct 2025, annuity issuer); Micruity ($5.1M seed, annuities in 401(k)s, undated); Blueprint Income (MassMutual subsidiary). Term life is crowded (Ladder, Bestow, Policygenius from background knowledge); annuity back-office is thin.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Best-interest documentation and suitability workflow for IMOs and carriers (compliance budget exists). 2) In-force book management for agents: maturity and surrender-expiry alerts plus 1035-exchange paperwork, if the 2022-24 purchase wave is maturing (needs verification). 3) Shared carrier contracting and licensing back-office network (agents wait weeks per carrier).
pools.insider_roles: IMO/FMO compliance officers; annuity wholesalers at carriers; independent agents with 500+ clients; IMO new-business desk staff; state insurance department market-conduct examiners; annuity actuaries.

pools.name: Wholesale, MGA and delegated-authority intermediation of US surplus lines (E&S) and specialty insurance
pools.size_basis: DERIVED. AM Best: US surplus lines direct premium $143.3B in 2025 (+10.4%), 12.9% of all P&C premium, 27.5% of commercial lines; surplus lines wrote over $51B of GL (39% of industry GL). Conning via InsurTech NY (secondary): US MGA premium about $128B in 2025. Assuming roughly 15% intermediary take on $143.3B gives about $21B. Cross-check: Ryan Specialty 2025 revenue $3,051M (+21.3%), about $1.4B (47%) delegated authority, implying about 14% share of a $21B pool.
pools.money_flow: Retail agents hand risks to wholesalers (Amwins, CRC/Ryan, Brown & Brown, Gallagher) and MGAs, who place with surplus lines carriers or fronting carriers supplying the balance sheet. Intermediaries are paid commission and fees by carriers out of premium.
pools.shock: The E&S double-digit boom is ending: premium growth slowed to 9.7% through Q3 2025 from 13.5%; competition in cyber, property and D&O; admitted carriers returning to lines they left; AM Best cut the segment outlook to stable in Nov 2025 and flagged adverse-development risk at fronting carriers (accident years 2021-2024). About 65 carriers formed or refocused on E&S in the past decade hold about 26% of premium (ALIRT). AXA XL is forming a wholesale-only surplus lines carrier for 2027.
pools.incumbents: Ryan Specialty ($3.05B revenue, #2 US wholesale, #1 delegated underwriter), Amwins, Brown & Brown, Gallagher, CRC; thousands of MGAs; capacity providers (Berkshire, Lloyd's, AIG, Markel, fronting carriers). Money is a percentage of premium.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Commission is a percentage of premium, so falling property rates shrink revenue while submission handling stays manual (each carrier has a portal and ACORD forms).
