Roughly 65 new E&S carriers must audit, bordereau-check and police dozens of MGAs by hand. Capacity providers can pull an MGA's support overnight. Surplus lines tax and stamping rules differ per state.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Sixfold ($30M Series B, Jan 2026, underwriting AI); Kalepa ($14M Series A plus an SMB MGA buildout); Corgi (AI-native carrier for startups, reported $2.6B valuation and further raises); Federato (no 2026 funding found). Underwriting-workbench AI is crowded and excluded by round-2 rules; the delegated-authority plumbing has no funded entrant found.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Bordereaux and delegated-authority compliance infrastructure sold to capacity providers and fronting carriers (budget line in underwriting management; AM Best's fronting concern raises stakes). 2) Surplus lines tax, diligent-search and stamping compliance as a service for wholesalers and MGAs. 3) MGA-capacity marketplace and orphan-program transfer when a capacity provider exits.
pools.insider_roles: MGA COOs and finance leads; bordereaux analysts; delegated-authority audit heads at carriers; wholesalers' submission-desk managers; program managers at fronting carriers; surplus lines compliance officers.

pools.name: US P&C insurers' claims-handling (adjusting) and litigation-defense expense (LAE)
pools.size_basis: DERIVED FROM PRIMARY DATA. Triple-I table (NAIC data via S&P): 2025 net premiums earned $959.5B; adjusting and other expense 5.3% (about $50.9B) plus defense and cost containment 3.7% (about $35.5B) = about $86.4B. 2024: 5.5% and 3.8% of $902.4B. NAIC separately reports $162.9B of unpaid LAE reserves.
pools.money_flow: Insurers' claims departments pay independent adjusters, TPAs and in-house staff (A&O) and defense law firms, experts and court costs (DCC). Estimating, repair-network and photo vendors are paid per claim.
pools.shock: 2025 Palisades and Eaton fires (costliest wildfires in world history, nearly half of 2025 insured losses in one state) plus severe convective storms of about $50B for the third straight year. AM Best says social inflation, nuclear verdicts and third-party litigation financing keep pressure on liability lines. CDI's Aug 2026 brief warns of a Super El Niño. Adjusting expense fell from 7.4% of premium (2021) to 5.3% (2025) in benign years, so surge capacity is thin.
pools.incumbents: In-house claims organizations; Sedgwick, Crawford, Gallagher Bassett and other TPAs/independent adjusters; Verisk (Xactimate), CCC and Enlyte for estimating; panel defense firms under billing guidelines; e-billing platforms such as CounselLink and Mitratech (named from background knowledge). Money is earned per file, per hour and per estimate.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Labor-intensive and volume-priced, so benign years cut staff and cat years overwhelm it. Panel-counsel bills are audited by hand. The payer (claims VP) is cost-pressured and no vendor owns litigation-spend intelligence.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session but funding is old: Five Sigma ($12M Series A 2021, $18M total), Snapsheet (over $100M raised, last round 2021). Named in a 2026 vendor guide with no 2023-2026 funding found: Tractable, CLARA Analytics, Hi Marley, Sprout.ai. Claims AI is a round-1 cliche and crowded; carrier-side litigation-spend intelligence has no funded entrant found.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Litigation-spend and panel-counsel performance intelligence (outcomes by firm and venue, not just bills) sold to claims VPs and litigation managers. 2) Credentialed catastrophe surge-capacity marketplace for adjusters and repair contractors, activated by event and paid per claim. 3) Subrogation and recovery services where insurers under-collect (needs sizing first).
pools.insider_roles: Claims VPs and litigation managers; cat adjusters; TPA operations heads; panel-counsel partners who bill hourly; Xactimate estimators and public adjusters; subrogation specialists; repair contractors.

pools.name: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
pools.geography: Global for cyber; US for the general liability base
pools.size_basis: Munich Re: global cyber premium $15.3B in 2024, about $16.3B in 2025, about $29B forecast for 2027. Larger base affected: US general liability about $131B (my derivation: surplus lines wrote $51B+ of GL, which AM Best says is 39% of industry GL). AI-specific spend today is a small fraction of both; the point is that AI coverage is being removed from existing policies so buyers must buy it elsewhere.
pools.money_flow: Corporates pay cyber, tech E&O, D&O and GL premiums; carriers pay claims and rely on Verisk/ISO form language shared across the market.
pools.shock: Verisk/ISO generative-AI exclusions took effect January 2026 (CG 40 47 broad, CG 40 48 advertising injury, CG 35 08 products). W.R. Berkley filed an 'absolute' AI exclusion across D&O, E&O and fiduciary; AIG, Great American and Hamilton filed exclusions; Beazley and QBE use AI sublimits of about 10% of cyber limits. An unverified analysis counts 2,369 generative-AI exclusion records across 49 states by mid-2026.
pools.incumbents: Chubb, AXA XL, Beazley, AIG, Travelers, Munich Re; cyber MGAs such as Coalition, At-Bay, Cowbell, Resilience (background knowledge); Verisk as form-maker; brokers Marsh and Aon.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Carriers cannot price AI risk (no loss history, no testing standard), so they exclude. Broad 'arising out of' wording leaves enterprises with deployments their own customers' contracts require them to insure. Forms are shared by licensing, so everyone excludes at once.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Armilla AI ($25M, Jan 2026, first Lloyd's coverholder dedicated to AI liability); Klaimee ($5.5M seed, Jul 2026, YC, insurance-backed performance warranties and A-F certification for AI agents); Mount (YC Spring 2026, AI-liability carrier, seed size unconfirmed); Corgi (AI-native carrier). Not verified: AIUC, Testudo, Vouch, and the cyber MGAs above.
pools.wedge_hints: 1) AI-system testing and certification standard that underwriters accept for pricing, paid by AI vendors because their customers demand insurance (Klaimee and Armilla already point here, so differentiate on testing depth and a shared standard). 2) M&A and renewal coverage-gap diligence, since acquirers inherit AI liabilities and see narrowed coverage only at renewal. 3) Pooled AI-incident loss-data consortium that gives actuaries something to price from.
pools.insider_roles: Policyholder-side coverage counsel; cyber and tech E&O underwriters at Beazley, Chubb, AXA XL; Verisk/ISO form drafters; broker cyber and tech practice leaders; CISOs and general counsel negotiating AI vendor contracts; cyber reinsurance modelers.

pools.name: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
pools.geography: Global (Vermont, Delaware, Bermuda, Cayman, Guernsey, Montana; 30+ US states have captive laws)
pools.size_basis: Marsh Benchmarking Report (published 2026-06-01): Marsh-managed captives wrote $79.1B gross written premium in 2025 ($77B in 2024). Swiss Re Institute's older estimate for the whole world was $60-80B, so the true total is at least Marsh's slice. The fee pool inside this (management, fronting, letters of credit, actuarial, reinsurance placement) is much smaller: at an assumed 3-5% it would be $2-4B (hypothesis, unsourced).
pools.money_flow: Corporates and groups of mid-size firms pay premium into their own insurance subsidiary instead of commercial carriers. Fronting carriers issue the policies and charge fees and collateral; managers (Marsh, Aon, WTW, Gallagher/Artex) charge management fees; reinsurers take the excess.
pools.shock: Captives kept growing as commercial pricing fell: Marsh-managed captive premium rose while its commercial price index fell 4% in 2025; Marsh formed 118 new captives in 2025 versus 92 in 2024 and manages about 1,500; third-party-risk captives wrote $4.4B; protected-cell programs grew 47% by premium. Regulatory moves: IRS final rule of 2025-01-14 listing certain 831(b) micro-captive transactions was upheld by one court in March 2026 (CIC Services) and narrowed in April 2026 (Drake Plastics) per conflicting secondary reports; Montana passed a new captive law in May 2025.
pools.incumbents: Marsh Captive Solutions, Aon, WTW, Gallagher/Artex; fronting carriers; group-captive specialists such as Captive Resources (background knowledge).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Conflict of interest: brokers earning commissions on commercial placements run the captives that replace them, so they sell captives to large clients and under-serve mid-size ones. Fronting capacity and letters of credit are costly and slow; domiciles are fragmented; no standard 'captive in a box' exists for a 20-100 unit fleet or contractor group.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found with 2023-2026 venture funding for captive management, fronting or group-captive formation. Searched: group captive, fronting fee, captive management, 831(b). One vendor guide says a 20-100 truck fleet needs about $50K-$250K initial capital (marketing estimate).
pools.wedge_hints: 1) Group-captive formation for 20-100 unit fleets, contractors and dealerships with standardized fronting, reinsurance and actuarial work (links to the trucking pool). 2) Captive loss-data benchmarking and feasibility studies as a data asset. 3) White-label cells (protected cell or rent-a-captive) for associations wanting a risk pool without building one. 'Open' on the venture side does not mean easy: heavy capital and regulatory moat.
pools.insider_roles: Captive managers; captive actuaries; Vermont, Delaware, Montana and Bermuda regulators; tax counsel from the 831(b) cases; fronting-carrier underwriters; group-captive agents; CFOs of mid-size trucking and construction firms.

pools.name: US data centers' spend on onsite / behind-the-meter power (engines, turbines, fuel cells, batteries, backup) and the services around it
pools.geography: United States (global figure ~$18B in 2026 shown for reference)
pools.size_basis: DERIVED. Enverus forecasts 22.5 GW of behind-the-meter generation for data centers in 2026-2030, about 4.5 GW/yr; at an assumed blended installed cost of $1.5-2.5M/MW (my assumption: recips low end, turbines and fuel cells high end) that is $7-11B/yr, midpoint ~$9B. Cross-checks: MarketsandMarkets (paid) global onsite/BTM data-center power ~$18B in 2026 rising to $87B by 2032; Baker Hughes >$25B BTM/off-grid opportunity by 2030. Reality check: Cleanview counts ~90 GW in the pipeline but only ~2 GW operating mid-2026 (mostly xAI Memphis), 5-13 GW by end-2027, so the pool is large on paper and slow in practice.
pools.money_flow: Hyperscalers, neoclouds and colos (or developers like Crusoe on their behalf) pay engine/turbine/fuel-cell OEMs, EPC and electrical contractors, gas suppliers and pipeline-lateral builders, and increasingly 'power-as-a-service' owners who finance and operate the plant (Bloom/Brookfield model). Utilities lose the load or the rate-base growth.
pools.shock: Heavy-duty gas turbine and grid-interconnection scarcity pushes buyers onsite. GE Vernova's gas backlog plus slot reservations hit 116 GW at Q2 2026 with 2031 delivery slots being sold; Caterpillar power generation grew 72% on data-center demand (per MarketsandMarkets). DOE asked FERC for a large-load interconnection rule by 2026-04-30; FERC instead opened six FPA 206 show-cause proceedings on 2026-06-18 (only confirmed at that level of detail). Texas SB 6 (2025-06-20) requires large loads >=75 MW to disclose backup generation and accept emergency curtailment.
pools.incumbents: Caterpillar, Cummins, Wartsila, GE Vernova (aeroderivatives), Siemens Energy, Solar Turbines, Bloom Energy (Brookfield financing framework expanded to $25B in June 2026; a framework, not booked revenue), EPC firms and gas midstream capture the money by selling equipment and installation.
pools.incumbent_fragility: OEMs are supply-capped, not demand-capped, so they cannot absorb more orders; utilities cannot deliver power on a data-center timeline. The scarce inputs are permits, engineering hours, commissioning crews and fuel supply, not money. Air-permit exposure is real: EPA reportedly found (Jan 2026, secondary report) that xAI's 'temporary/portable' Memphis turbines are not exempt; the county permit for 15 turbines expires 2027-01-02.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Crusoe (Series E $1.375B Oct 2025; Series F ~$3B+ at ~$30B valuation, reported closed Sept 2026), Bloom Energy (public), ProEnergy (private; repurposed CF6 jet-engine cores, 21 turbines sold for >1 GW of data-center bridging power), Emerald AI ($150M Series A at $1.05B, 2026-08-25; makes data centers flexible loads), DG Matrix ($60M Series A, Feb 2026; ~90% of pipeline is data centers). VoltaGrid is a named private provider but its funding was not verified.
pools.wedge_hints: Air-permit and emissions-compliance engineering for onsite turbines/engines; commissioning and controls integration (islanded microgrids with grid-forming batteries); gas supply and lateral procurement; bridging-power rental fleets; secondary-market and refurbished-core brokerage; replacing diesel backup under tightening air limits. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): permitting + commissioning + controls is ~300 campuses x $300k = ~$90M; reaching $100M+ most plausibly means owning assets or financing, which is the crowded layer.
pools.insider_roles: Data-center development VPs of power; utility large-load account managers; air-permit consultants; OEM dealer application engineers; interconnection consultants; midstream gas marketers.

pools.name: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
pools.size_basis: Commercial (paid) estimates disagree: MarketsandMarkets $13.76B in 2025 rising to $19.0B by 2030; Arizton $16.5B (2024); GMI $12.2B (2024); narrow-definition outliers $0.7-3.4B. I used the broad definition (~$14B). Cross-check: EEI transmission capex $39.9B (2025 projected) and distribution capex $50.9B (2023), so $14B is plausibly 10-15% of grid capex. Wood Mackenzie: imports ~80% of power-transformer and ~50% of distribution-transformer supply in 2025.
pools.money_flow: Utilities (close to half of distribution-transformer demand in one global forecast), IPPs/developers, data centers and industrials pay manufacturers and electrical distributors; most units are imported.
pools.shock: Section 232 tariffs took effect 2025-08-18 (50% on the non-US steel/aluminum content of transformers). Wood Mackenzie projected 2025 supply deficits of 30% (power) and 10% (distribution); generator step-up lead times passed 160 weeks by Q1 2026; DOE cites >30 months for distribution units; ~40M US distribution transformers are past expected service life; only one US grain-oriented steel producer (Cleveland-Cliffs).
pools.incumbents: Hitachi Energy (>$1B US investment announced 2025-09-04; $457M Virginia large-power-transformer plant broke ground June 2026, operating 2H 2028), Siemens Energy, GE Vernova (closed $5.3B buyout of Prolec GE on 2026-02-02; Prolec 2025 revenue ~$3B), Eaton, Hubbell and regional makers; distributors resell.
pools.incumbent_fragility: New capacity does not arrive until 2027-2028; grain-oriented steel is single-sourced; every utility has custom specs, which blocks standard-unit mass production; utilities hold spares in silos. Manufacturers have cyclical-capex scars and no reason to over-build, so they cannot respond quickly.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: All solid-state-transformer hardware: Heron Power ($140M Series B, Feb 2026, a16z American Dynamism + Breakthrough; $38M Series A in 2025; 40 GW plant, production 2H 2027), DG Matrix ($60M Series A, Feb 2026), Amperesand ($80M Series A, late 2025), Hyperscale Power (EUR 5M seed, Mar 2026). None found funded on repair/refurbishment, spares pooling or spec standardization (searched solid-state and general terms only; 'none found', not 'none exist').
pools.wedge_hints: Transformer repair/rewind and life extension for the ~40M units past service life; mutualized spares pool or group purchasing for ~2,000 public-power utilities and ~800+ co-ops (approximate counts, unverified); standard-spec consortium to aggregate orders into factory slots; condition-monitoring analytics; certified used-transformer marketplace with test data; tariff/import-compliance brokerage. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): a consortium brokering ~$2-3B/yr of co-op and muni purchases at 3-4% is $60-120M.
pools.insider_roles: Utility transformer asset managers; co-op and muni procurement directors; transformer repair-shop owners; distributor reps (Graybar/Wesco type); transformer test labs; NRECA/APPA purchasing staff.

pools.name: US electric utilities' vegetation management (line clearance and tree trimming)
pools.size_basis: Power Magazine (post-LA fires, Jan 2025) estimates ~$7B/yr; Harris Williams (2022 report) via Middle Market Growth estimates ~$8B/yr and calls it often the largest utility O&M line item; midpoint ~$7.5B. Cross-check (DERIVED): Davey Tree's utility segment grew $54.2M (+5.4%) in 2025, implying ~$1.06B segment revenue; Asplundh is private (~$4.7B revenue in 2021 per Wikipedia, single-source, low confidence). Other reports claim $8.2B (US-ish) to $30B (global) and are paid-report quality.
pools.money_flow: Utilities pay line-clearance contractors (Asplundh, Davey, Wright Tree, Lewis, ACRT and others) by unit price, crew-hour or per-mile; costs are recovered from ratepayers as O&M. Inspection and LiDAR vendors sit on top.
pools.shock: Wildfire liability became existential and visible: Xcel agreed to pay ~$640M for the Marshall Fire (2025-09-24); SCE booked $1.6B of Eaton Fire losses by 2026-06-30 and exhausted self-insurance on 2026-02-11 (outside Jefferies estimate of exposure: $13.5B); PacifiCorp was found grossly negligent for Oregon's 2020 fires. California SB 254 (Sept 2025) requires cost-per-avoided-ignition reporting, pushing utilities from fixed-cycle trimming toward risk-based trimming.
pools.incumbents: Asplundh (private), Davey Tree (public), Wright Tree, Lewis Tree, ACRT, plus engineering/LiDAR firms, capture the money by selling crew-hours and unit-priced work.
pools.incumbent_fragility: They sell crew-hours, so analytics that cut crew-hours threaten their revenue (business-model conflict); little software culture; utility foresters often manage work in spreadsheets and GIS exports. Spend verification is weak (who trimmed what, to which clearance, at what price), and cycle-based schedules are indefensible after Marshall/Eaton while regulators want cost-effectiveness proof the incumbents' data cannot supply.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Overstory ($43M Series B, Nov 2025, Blume-led with Energy Impact Partners and B Capital; $14M Series A in 2023). Adjacent: Pano AI (camera detection, $44M Series B, $89M total, 15 utilities incl. Xcel) and Gridware ($55M Series B 2025-11-17; $26.4M Series A Jan 2025, Sequoia). Nobody found funded on work verification, invoice audit, crew marketplaces or small-utility foresters.
pools.wedge_hints: Work-verification and unit-price invoice audit for utility VM spend; crew scheduling and subcontractor marketplace with storm-surge staffing; hazard-tree identification for the highest-risk circuits; herbicide-program verification; co-ops and munis with no staff forester. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): audit/verification software at 1-2% of a $7.5B pool is $75-150M only if it reaches most large IOUs; a crew marketplace taking 5% of subcontract flow is bigger but operationally harder.
pools.insider_roles: Utility vegetation managers and ISA-certified utility arborists; line-clearance general foremen; contractor estimators; wildfire-plan regulatory staff; forestry GIS analysts; insurance risk engineers.

pools.name: US utility wildfire mitigation programs (undergrounding, covered conductor, sensing, inspection, PSPS), California-led
pools.geography: United States (California-led; also CO, OR, UT and other Western states)
pools.size_basis: DERIVED. PG&E alone: 2025 wildfire mitigation spending estimated >$6B (PNNL May 2025, citing PG&E). The two California IOUs' wildfire mitigation plans were reported to detail >$23B of expenditures through 2025 (about $7.7B/yr over 2023-25 combined; source is a Buchalter title I could not open). Add Xcel ($1.9B proposed 2025-27 in Colorado alone), Berkshire Hathaway Energy (wildfire capex rising from $188M in 2022 to $797M in 2027), PacifiCorp, SDG&E and others to reach ~$9B. Capital is 55-86% of the spend across four utilities that split it.
pools.money_flow: Ratepayers fund utilities (capex into rate base); utilities pay EPC/line contractors, equipment makers (covered conductor, fast-trip protection), sensor/software vendors and vegetation contractors; the California Wildfire Fund backstops liability.
pools.shock: California SB 254 (signed Sept 2025) adds an $18B Wildfire Fund continuation account (half ratepayer via an extended charge, half shareholders; PG&E 47.85%, SCE 47.85%, SDG&E 4.3%), bars $6B of wildfire-mitigation capex from earning a return in rate base, requires cost-per-avoided-ignition reporting, and exempts undergrounding plan approvals from CEQA. Utilities lose return on part of the spend, so cheaper and provably effective measures win.
pools.incumbents: The utilities themselves, EPC contractors (Quanta, MasTec), equipment OEMs and engineering firms capture the money.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Regulation now demands a metric (cost per avoided ignition) that nobody has a standard methodology or data for, and return on $6B of spend was removed, flipping incentives toward cost-effective options. Liability rules can still move: an August 2026 tentative ruling declined to hold SCE liable without a trial (trial set for 2027).
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Pano AI ($44M Series B, $89M total, 15 utilities), Gridware ($55M Series B, Nov 2025), Overstory ($43M Series B, Nov 2025). Other fire-modeling vendors exist but were not verified. Detection/sensing is the busy layer.
pools.wedge_hints: Cost-per-avoided-ignition analytics and wildfire-plan compliance reporting; PSPS customer notification plus medical-baseline backup-power logistics; inspection QA (drone/ground); covered-conductor install productivity; wildfire plans for Western co-ops and munis that must now file them. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): analytics/compliance software at 1% of $9B is only ~$90M, so reaching $100M needs a services or logistics layer.
pools.insider_roles: Utility wildfire-mitigation program managers; PSPS incident commanders; fire-weather meteorologists; state energy-safety regulators; insurance brokers; covered-conductor crew leads.

pools.name: PJM capacity payments passed through to utilities' and large customers' bills
pools.size_basis: PJM's 2028/29 delivery-year Base Residual Auction (results 2026-07-14) cleared at the $325/MW-day cap, procuring 138,318 MW for a total cost of $16.4B. Without the cap PJM estimated ~$555/MW-day, roughly $30B. The independent market monitor attributes $6.3B (38%) to data centers. Each verified megawatt of flexibility is worth ~$118k/yr at the cap (325 x 365, DERIVED).
pools.money_flow: Generators and demand-response providers are paid at the clearing price; load-serving entities (utilities and retail suppliers) charge customers. For large customers the share is set by their peak load contribution, which (from my knowledge of PJM rules, not re-verified here) is based on load at the system's summer coincident peaks, so curtailing at the right hours cuts the capacity charge.
pools.shock: Auction results released 2026-07-14: third straight year at the cap, 6,831 MW short of PJM's reliability target. The price collar (cap $325, floor $175) was extended through the December 2026 auction for 2029/30; PJM planned to ask FERC in September for a backstop procurement (outcome not confirmed).
pools.incumbents: Demand-response aggregators (CPower and others), retail energy suppliers, utilities, and brokers/consultants paid on commodity commissions capture the pass-through and DR fees.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Legacy DR products are mostly emergency-only on fixed contracts, and market rules on DR performance and ELCC derating keep shifting, which punishes fixed portfolios. Brokers earn on volume, not on demand reduction. Most mid-size customers (1-20 MW) do not manage their peak at all even though a managed megawatt is worth ~$118k/yr at the cap.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Voltus ($225M Series D, 2026, Vitol; claims 8.1 GW of flexible capacity managed, a 100 MW Google deal in PJM, acquired Brightfield AI in June 2026), Emerald AI ($150M Series A at $1.05B, 2026-08-25). EnergyHub, Renew Home and Base Power are plausible competitors but their funding was not verified.
pools.wedge_hints: Mid-market C&I peak-tag management with batteries and controls; coincident-peak prediction and alerts; capacity-pass-through audits of large customers' supplier contracts; school, hospital and muni aggregation; data-center flexible-load contracting. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): 5,000 PJM customers each avoiding $50-100k of annual capacity cost with the vendor keeping 25-30% gives $60-150M; needs software plus storage financing.
pools.insider_roles: C&I energy managers; retail-supplier pricing desks; PJM market-monitor analysts; DR dispatch operators; utility rate analysts; data-center power procurement leads.

pools.name: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
pools.geography: Global (US share ~$4.5B per GMI); the US fleet is central to the shock
pools.size_basis: GMI (paid report): $27.1B in 2025 and $30.2B in 2026, US $4.5B. Other paid reports range $10-25B depending on scope (Future Market Report $10.25B; MarkNtel all-turbine services $25.3B in 2026, gas ~46%). Filing cross-check: GE Vernova's Power services revenue was $13.07B in 2025 (gas, steam, nuclear and hydro together; not split) against $6.42B of equipment. Siemens Energy Gas Services ~EUR 1.6B in FY2025 (unconfirmed whether revenue or profit). Treat as a $10-30B range, ~$30B at the top.
pools.money_flow: Plant owners (utilities, IPPs, industrials, data-center BTM operators) pay OEMs through long-term service agreements (LTSAs), parts and outage services; independent service providers and repair shops take a minority (top 5 firms hold ~39% of global services per MarkNtel).
pools.shock: GE Vernova's gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations rose from 100 to 116 GW in Q2 2026 (target >=125 GW by year-end), it is selling 2031 slots, and output is 20 GW/yr rising to 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030. New heavy-duty units are unavailable for years, so owners must keep old frames running, defer retirements and lengthen overhaul cycles, while BTM data-center adds enlarge the fleet needing service.
pools.incumbents: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi, Solar/Baker Hughes, Ansaldo capture the money via LTSAs, proprietary hot-gas-path parts and outage services; a thin layer of independent service providers.
pools.incumbent_fragility: OEMs prioritize scarce factory and field-service capacity for new equipment (business-model conflict with servicing old units cheaply); outage labor is short; parts lead times are long; owners have little price transparency on LTSAs. Proprietary designs lock parts, but also leave gaps where owners cannot get service slots.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found focused on turbine MRO/parts after two broad searches (treat as open but confirm with named-company checks before building). Adjacent: ProEnergy (private) selling repurposed CF6 jet-engine cores for data-center power.
pools.wedge_hints: LTSA and parts-price benchmarking and audit for owners; condition-based outage planning (borescope AI, digital twins); a certified marketplace for surplus frames, aeroderivatives and spare parts including slot transfers; outage-technician staffing and credentialing; rotable inventory pooling among IPPs and co-ops; independent hot-gas-path repair (capital intensive). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): benchmarking/audit at 1% of a ~$20B accessible pool is $200M but early capture is a fraction; surplus-equipment brokerage at 3-5% of a few $B/yr of trades reaches $100M+ only if scarcity persists.
pools.insider_roles: Plant O&M directors at IPPs and utilities; outage managers; combustion engineers; LTSA contract managers; ex-OEM field service reps; independent service-provider shop owners; insurer engineering surveyors.

pools.name: US oil and gas operators' produced-water gathering, disposal, recycling and treatment
pools.size_basis: DERIVED. Rystad's 2022 outlook put US onshore produced water at 22.9B bbl in 2022 and 23.8B bbl in 2026; times an assumed blended all-in cost of $0.40-0.65/bbl (B3 Insights says Delaware-basin gathering plus disposal will reach $0.75-1.00/bbl; Aris reports $0.31-0.46/bbl margin on top of its own costs) gives ~$9-15B, midpoint ~$12B. Broader benchmark: Bluefield (Oct 2025) sizes US midstream water at $156B over 2025-2030 (~$26B/yr, Permian $101.8B), which includes freshwater sourcing and frac-water logistics.
pools.money_flow: E&P operators pay water-midstream companies per barrel for pipeline gathering and saltwater-disposal (SWD) injection, and trucking firms for spot loads; a small and growing fraction goes to treatment and recycling.
pools.shock: The Texas Railroad Commission widened the area of review for new SWD permits from a quarter mile to half a mile (from 2025-06-01), added injection-pressure and volume limits tied to reservoir pressure, and barred deep injection below the top of the Strawn in the Gardendale seismic response area; at least one-third of Permian SWD wells have lost injection capacity since 2016; B3 sees 20-30% cost increases in parts of the Delaware. In 2026 the escape valve (treated-water discharge) is still blocked: TCEQ has issued no discharge permits since accepting applications in 2024, and the early-2026 land-application rule drew ~450 comments with over two-thirds opposed (Aug 2026).
pools.incumbents: Aris Water, WaterBridge (raised $345M equity), Texas Pacific Water Resources, NGL, Select Water; many E&Ps run their own SWD systems. The business is acreage dedication plus fixed pipes and wells.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Disposal capacity is constrained by physics and regulation, not by capital; pipes and wells cannot be software-updated; treatment is energy-hungry (the Orla plant needs 5.5 MW for 10,000 bbl/d) and has no outlet permits. Wood Mackenzie projects $3-6 of water cost per barrel of oil over time, so incumbents cannot escape the regulatory ceiling.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Axine Water Technologies ($5.6M Series A, Oct 2025), Sourcewater ($7.2M Series A, water data/market; date unverified), Clean Chemistry ($2.2M; date unverified), WaterTectonics + Clearvale's WT Oil & Gas (launched Oct 2025). All small compared with the infrastructure incumbents.
pools.wedge_hints: SWD pressure-front and seismic-risk analytics for operators and regulators; disposal-capacity and recycled-water marketplace; trucking dispatch and verification; SWD integrity monitoring; permitting service for reuse; matching treated water to data-center cooling or agriculture once discharge rules open. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): a capacity marketplace/software layer taking 2-3% of a $12B pool is $240-360M at full share, but traction needs operators to give up self-disposal; a data/compliance product alone is likely under $100M. Legal premise to check: induced-seismicity rules and produced-water ownership (Texas moved land-application authority from RRC to TCEQ in 2025).
pools.insider_roles: E&P water and completions managers; water-midstream commercial managers; RRC/TCEQ permit consultants; SWD operators; hydrogeologists and seismologists; surface-use landmen; water-trucking dispatchers.

pools.name: US nuclear fleet operating, fuel and capital spend (and the outsourced supplier/services ecosystem behind it)
pools.size_basis: DERIVED. 816 TWh generated in 2024 (World Nuclear Association) x $31.76/MWh total generating cost (NEI/EUCG 2023 dollars: fuel $5.32, capital $7.06, operating $19.38 per MWh) = ~$25.9B; operating cost alone is ~$15.8B. Uses 2023 cost data with 2024 generation; no newer NEI edition was found.
pools.money_flow: About two dozen owner-operators (Constellation, Vistra, Duke, Southern, Dominion, Entergy and others) pay fuel suppliers, O&M labor, outage-services firms (Westinghouse, Framatome, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, Jacobs, Bechtel and specialists), engineers (Sargent & Lundy is ENR's #1 nuclear-plant design firm), compliance and NRC fees. Hyperscaler PPAs now fund uprates and restarts.
pools.shock: Executive Order 14300 (2025-05-23) sets 18-month limits for new-reactor decisions and 12-month limits for license renewals, with NRC final rules due ~November 2026 and an NRC reorganization. Follow-through: NRC approved TVA's Clinch River BWRX-300 construction permit on 2026-09-29 (14-month review), TerraPower's Natrium permit in March 2026, four DOE pilot test reactors reached criticality by 2026-07-04, and Palisades began fuel loading (~2026-08-31) after repeated slips.
pools.incumbents: Owner-operators' in-house staff plus the OEM/outage-services oligopoly capture the money; documentation, quality assurance (NQA-1) and condition-report workflows are largely manual.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Aging workforce; regulatory documentation (licensing responses, 10 CFR 50.59 screenings, condition reports) is mostly hand-written; very few shops hold nuclear quality certifications, so the new-build and uprate wave hits a supplier base that cannot scale; commercial-grade dedication is slow and expensive. QA sign-offs cannot be waived by software.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, Sept 2025, Blue Bear; claims >65 reactors; per-reactor annual subscription) and Atomic Canyon ($7M seed, May 2025, Energy Impact Partners; Diablo Canyon customer). Both target documentation/AI search, not supplier qualification, staffing or outage services. Reactor developers (Valar, Aalo, Antares, Deployable Energy) are funded but do not attack fleet spend.
pools.wedge_hints: Nuclear supplier qualification and commercial-grade dedication marketplace; outage workforce staffing and credentialing (radiation-worker portability); counterfeit/suspect-item detection; procurement of nuclear-grade valves and pumps; uprate engineering at scale; restart and decommissioning services; licensing documentation (contested). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): if outsourced services and supplies are ~40% of the pool (~$10B), a staffing/qualification marketplace taking 5% is ~$500M at full share; $100M needs ~20% of that, a stretch without a standard or certification role.
pools.insider_roles: Plant licensing engineers; outage managers; procurement and commercial-grade dedication engineers; NQA-1 lead auditors; radiation protection technicians; fuel reload engineers; former NRC resident inspectors.

pools.name: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
pools.size_basis: Floor figure, annualized from one contractor. Quanta Services' Electric segment booked $7.84B revenue in Q2 2026 (+44% y/y), ~$31B annualized (DERIVED); this excludes MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Henkels & McCoy, Asplundh's utility work and engineering firms. Payer budget: EEI projects $208B of investor-owned-utility capex in 2025 (>$1.1T for 2025-2029), with transmission $39.9B (2025) and distribution $50.9B (2023). Engineering/design is a smaller slice; no sourced engineering share was found (an NYISO independent estimate puts a mixed bucket of mobilization, engineering, permitting, testing, project management and indirects at ~28% of one line's subtotal).
pools.money_flow: IOUs, co-ops, munis, RTOs and data-center/renewable developers pay line contractors (Quanta, MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Henkels) and engineering firms (Burns & McDonnell is ENR's #1 power design firm, Sargent & Lundy #3; also Black & Veatch, POWER Engineers, Ulteig, Kimley-Horn). Utility capex is recovered through rates.
pools.shock: Quanta's Q2 2026 revenue was $9.56B (vs $6.77B a year earlier), total backlog $53.4B, 2026 guidance raised to $39.3-39.7B, and it added ~7,400 employees through four acquisitions in the quarter and July; more meaningful field activity on some newly booked projects is expected from 2H 2027. EEI's capex plan and data-center load growth are the drivers; the lineworker and engineer shortage is widely cited but no 2026 source was found.
pools.incumbents: Quanta, MasTec, MYR on construction; Burns & McDonnell, Sargent & Lundy, Black & Veatch on engineering. They bill by the hour or unit and design still runs on utility-specific standards and desktop tools.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Growth is gated by hiring, not demand; automation reduces billable hours (business-model conflict); every utility's design standards differ; small utilities cannot compete for contractor crews.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Piq Energy ($5M seed, 2026-07-08; automates interconnection/grid-planning studies), Pearl Street Technologies (acquired by Enverus, Mar 2025), envelio (German; Eversource uses it). Nothing funded found on distribution design, estimating, crew productivity or lineworker workforce.
pools.wedge_hints: Distribution design automation for new-load service requests on utility GIS; estimating and bid tools for line contractors; crew scheduling, materials staging and yard logistics; mutual-assistance storm-staffing marketplace; lineworker apprenticeship and credentialing pipeline (a network/standard asset); outsourced 'engineer-in-a-box' for ~2,000 public-power utilities and ~800+ co-ops (approximate counts, unverified). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): design automation plus engineering-as-a-service for 200 mid-size utilities at $500k each is $100M; a workforce marketplace taking 3% of $30B+ is ~$1B at full share but a thin-margin labor business.
pools.insider_roles: Utility distribution planners and designers; line-construction superintendents; contractor estimators; T&D engineering managers; storm-response coordinators; IBEW/NECA training directors; project-controls managers.

pools.name: US industrial MRO and indirect-supplies spend by plants, contractors and facilities (industrial distribution)
pools.geography: United States (North America for Grainger's sizing)
pools.size_basis: Grainger's own 2022 investor-day estimate of its North American high-touch addressable market (about $165B; Grainger about 7% share or $11B) [secondary, via search summary, not re-verified]. Earlier 10-K sizing put US MRO at about $127B in 2017 and said no player has double-digit share. Cross-check from actuals [primary]: Grainger FY2025 net sales $17,942M at 39.1% gross margin and its 10-K calls MRO 'large and fragmented'; Fastenal 9M-2026 sales $7,051.9M (about $9.4B annualised, my derivation); MSC fiscal Q3-2026 sales $1,047M (about $4.2B annualised, my derivation). Top three are about $31B, a minority of the pool.
pools.money_flow: Plants, contractors and facilities pay industrial distributors (Grainger, Fastenal, MSC, Motion, Applied, Amazon Business, thousands of regional independents) for fasteners, safety gear, cutting tools, bearings, electrical and janitorial supplies. Distributors buy from thousands of suppliers (Grainger: 5,000+ primary suppliers, none above 5% of purchases) and earn roughly 39-45% gross margin.
pools.shock: Tariff regime churn plus spend consolidating to the largest distributors. IEEPA tariffs were struck down 2026-02-20; Section 232 metals tariffs were restructured 2026-04-02 (effective 2026-04-06); the 10% Section 122 surcharge expired 2026-07-24 and was replaced by Section 301 duties of 10%/12.5% on goods from 60 economies. Fastenal Q3-2026 (reported 2026-10-14): net sales $2,463.3M, +15.5%; pricing added about 240bp; customer sites fell to 90,759 from 98,823 while $50k+/month sites rose to 3,288 from 2,771; manufacturing daily sales +17.2%, heavy manufacturing +20.2%; gross margin helped by direct sourcing savings, supplier rebates and tariff refunds. Grainger said underlying MRO demand was muted in 2025.
pools.incumbents: Grainger, Fastenal, MSC, Applied Industrial, Motion, Amazon Business, Home Depot's SRS/HD Supply, plus a long tail of local and regional independent distributors. They capture the money through product margin (39-45% gross) plus inventory-management services (vending, bin stocking, onsite).
pools.incumbent_fragility: The big three are healthy, so they are not the fragile layer. The fragile layers are mid-size independent distributors (losing national accounts to Fastenal and Grainger, per the site-count shift, and repricing slowly while tariffs change every few months) and plants' own storerooms (large stocks of slow-moving spares they cannot find, cross-reference or sell). Amazon Business and Zoro compete on the low-touch tail.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Partium (Philadelphia, AI industrial spare-parts search, $15M Series A led by Trestle Partners, 2024-09); Eezee (Singapore, MRO e-commerce, $5M raised 2026-02, $18.7M total); Moglix (India, B2B industrial marketplace); GoExpedi (Houston, last round $25M Series B in 2019, so old). Amazon Business and Grainger's Zoro are the real competition. No US startup with a 2025-2026 round targeting independent distributors was found.
pools.wedge_hints: (a) Repricing and sourcing-substitution software for independent industrial distributors under tariff volatility; (b) plant-side spare-parts data cleanup, cross-reference and surplus resale; (c) distributor roll-ups where the acquirer supplies software and buying scale. Bottom-up hypothesis: about 2,000 independent distributors at $50k a year of software is $100M (count not verified).
pools.insider_roles: Plant storeroom and MRO buyers; inside sales reps and branch managers at independent distributors; Fastenal onsite managers; distributor pricing analysts; reliability and maintenance planners; indirect-spend category managers.

pools.name: US OEM spend on outsourced custom machined parts from independent machine shops
pools.size_basis: IBISWorld machine-shop services (NAICS 33271), updated Feb 2026: about $47.8B 2026 revenue, 16,619 businesses, about 224,000 employees, 0.4% five-year revenue CAGR [secondary, via search summary]. My derivation: about $2.9M revenue and 13.5 employees per business. Excludes captive in-house machining and fabricated-metal job shops. Xometry management's $275B custom-parts opportunity is a global company claim and was not used.
pools.money_flow: Aerospace, defense, energy, medical, machinery and automotive manufacturers buy custom machined parts from about 16,600 independent shops, mostly by RFQ and relationships; marketplaces (Xometry, Protolabs) take the prototype and low-volume end.
pools.shock: Section 232 metals tariffs restructured by proclamation 2026-04-02 (effective 2026-04-06): most derivatives moved from 50% on metal content to 25% on full entered value, the derivative-inclusions process was terminated, and Commerce/USTR can add products on a rolling basis; Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% added 2026-07-23/24. This changes landed cost of imported machined and fabricated parts and makes domestic quotes competitive, while NTMA surveys show recruitment is the top constraint for every respondent. Capital is flooding the defense niche (Hadrian $1.37B Series D in 2026).
pools.incumbents: Thousands of owner-operated machine shops; buyer-side OEM procurement and supplier-development teams; marketplaces Xometry (public) and Protolabs (public, in-house production); Fictiv and Hubs (acquired, per memory, not re-verified).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Shops quote by hand over days, are owner-led with an aging workforce, and cannot easily finance automation or absorb surge demand; skilled-machinist recruitment is the top NTMA concern. Marketplaces fit prototypes and low volume, not mid-volume production runs.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Xometry (public; Q3-2025 revenue $181.0M, +28%; a critic argues marketplace revenue flat since Q3-2022); Protolabs (public); Fictiv and Hubs (no recent round found); Hadrian ($260M in 2025-07, then $1.37B Series D in 2026 at $7.87B valuation, automated US factories for defense/space CNC parts); Isembard (London, reported $50M Series A led by Union Square Ventures in 2026, unverified); Standard Bots ($200M Series C June 2026, sells robots to machine shops). Crowded for defense/aerospace CNC, contested overall.
pools.wedge_hints: Mid-volume (100-5,000 piece), mid-tolerance parts that Xometry's prototype model and Hadrian's defense-grade model both skip; shop-side ERP, quoting, scheduling and inspection-as-a-service (CMM and first-article reports); buy-and-automate roll-ups of non-defense shops; used-machine and tooling financing. Bottom-up check: $100M of software needs about 2,000 shops at $50k (12% of all shops), which is heroic; a marketplace or roll-up route needs about $1B of flow at a 10% take.
pools.insider_roles: Shop owners and estimators; OEM sourcing and supplier-development engineers; NTMA and PMPA staff; CNC programmers; commercial and SBA lenders to shops; Haas and Mazak dealers.

pools.name: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
pools.size_basis: AFS (American Foundry Society, July 2026): US metalcasting industry revenue about $53.7B in 2025, with casting sales projected +8.0% in 2026 (about $58B), up from a 4.2% January projection [primary]. Forgings are not included; the only FIA figure found was $10.6B of custom-forging shipments in 2012, too old to use. Foundry count not found.
pools.money_flow: OEMs and defense primes (valves and fittings, pumps, heavy equipment, vehicles, rail, aerospace and defense) pay foundries for castings; foundries buy scrap, alloys, sand and patterns and do their own finishing.
pools.shock: The Department of War's Manufacturing Technology Program Strategic Plan FY2026-2031 (published 2026-09-30) names castings, forgings and microelectronics as single points of failure and states the department lacks latent capacity to rapidly scale production of key systems and munitions in a crisis, citing offshoring, consolidation, qualification delays and small-supplier financing gaps (no new dollars attached). A Pentagon acquisition official is quoted saying the defense cast-and-forge supply chain has shrunk 80% (date unclear), with at least 122,000 more workers needed by 2028. AFS puts tariff cost to the industry near $1B to date; a June 2026 MxD roadmap cites aging equipment and offshoring.
pools.incumbents: Thousands of small and mid-size foundries; large aerospace casting and forging houses (Howmet, PCC, Wyman-Gordon, Carpenter, from memory). About 377 foundries make valves and pipe fittings (narrower count).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Capital-intensive, environmentally permitted, aging workforce, long pattern and tooling lead times, and NADCAP/AS9100 qualification that takes months to years, so customers cannot easily dual-source and capacity is sticky and cannot flex to surge demand.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Fabri (MIT spinout, investment casting, $13.5M total, backed by RTX Ventures and Lockheed Martin Ventures, second foundry targeted for 2027; one profile dates a seed to 2026-06, likely a data artifact); Foundry Lab (New Zealand, microwave casting, $8M Series A, date unclear). Adjacent: Hadrian (CNC, not casting). No funded foundry-sourcing marketplace or qualification-as-a-service company found.
pools.wedge_hints: Casting and forging sourcing and qualification (RFQ routing, first-article, NADCAP-ready paperwork); pattern and tooling as-a-service (digital twin, 3D-printed sand molds); foundry capacity and utilisation data; casting-to-machining kitted supply for primes; foundry roll-up with software. Bottom-up check: a 3% take on $53.7B is about $1.6B of flow-based revenue, so $100M needs about 6% of the pool at 3% take; needs trust and qualification credentials first.
pools.insider_roles: Foundry owners, melt and pattern-shop managers; prime supplier-quality engineers; DCMA reps; NADCAP auditors; AFS and FIA staff; metallurgists qualifying alloys.

pools.name: DoD munitions and shipbuilding production-ramp dollars flowing to sub-tier suppliers
pools.size_basis: My derivation. OBBBA (signed 2025-07-04) gave about $150B for defense with execution to 2029, reported lines $29B shipbuilding and $25B munitions: $54B over about 4 years is about $13.5B a year; FY2026 appropriations (topline $838.7B) added roughly $3B-$6.4B for munitions (sources differ) plus multiyear authority for 8 of 13 missiles. Gross new procurement about $17-20B a year; an Army official said subcontractors often account for 50-60% of weapon-system cost, so sub-tier flow is about $9-12B a year; I use $10B. Full base-budget flow is larger but not sourced here. Line items are secondary (law-firm alert, SOFREP, Breaking Defense).
pools.money_flow: Congress funds the Department of War; primes (Lockheed, RTX, Northrop, General Dynamics, HII, L3Harris) pay roughly half or more of weapon-system cost to sub-tier suppliers for castings, forgings, machined parts, energetics and electronics.
pools.shock: OBBBA reconciliation funding (2025-07-04) with reporting that the Pentagon planned to spend it in FY2026; FY2026 appropriations (2026-02) gave multiyear authority for PAC-3, LRASM, JASSM-ER, THAAD, SM-6, AMRAAM, Tomahawk and SM-3 IB; a 2026 Iran campaign reportedly cost $33.4B including $22.3B of expended munitions (secondary, unverified) and exposed rocket-motor, energetics and labor bottlenecks. Lockheed said in May 2026 it will invest $8-9B through 2030 including new second sources; GMLRS rose from about 8,000 to about 14,000 rounds a year and PAC-3 from 300 to 550 missiles.
pools.incumbents: Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, HII, L3Harris, Boeing and their tier-1s, who capture the money through cost-plus and fixed-price multiyear contracts.
pools.incumbent_fragility: The Department of War itself says there is no latent capacity; supplier qualification cycles are long, many parts are sole-source, small suppliers face financing gaps, and primes cannot create sub-tier capacity by contract alone. The CMMC compliance route was reversed in July 2026 (Phase 2 suspended), showing small-supplier cost sensitivity.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Hadrian ($1.37B Series D 2026, $7.87B valuation); Isembard ($50M Series A 2026, unverified); Fabri ($13.5M, casting); from memory and not searched: Anduril, Castelion, Firehawk, X-Bow, Ursa Major, Saronic, Divergent. Crowded for capacity and hardware; open only for the support layer (supplier qualification, first-article inspection, special-process capacity).
pools.wedge_hints: AS9102 first-article inspection automation; special-process capacity brokerage (NADCAP heat treat, plating, NDT; a known aerospace bottleneck, from memory); sub-tier supplier-development services sold to primes; working-capital financing for small defense suppliers; sub-tier supply-chain mapping for DCMA and program offices. Legal premise to check: DFARS specialty-metals rules, ITAR, cost-accounting rules for subcontract financing.
pools.insider_roles: Prime supplier-development and supplier-quality engineers; DCMA industrial specialists; program-office industrial-base analysts; sub-tier shop owners with AS9100; NADCAP auditors.

pools.name: US industrial plant maintenance, repair and millwright labor and outsourced machinery repair
pools.size_basis: Outsourced: about $54.6B for NAICS 81131 (commercial and industrial machinery repair group), Economic Census 2022, as quoted by Vantage Insights [secondary, group-level; Census does not publish a separate 811310 total in what I could reach, and the Census API needed a key I did not register for]. In-house on top: BLS counts 547,300 jobs in 2025 (446,900 industrial machinery mechanics, 59,700 machinery maintenance workers, 40,700 millwrights) at median pay $64,100 [primary]; my derivation 547,300 x $64,100 = about $35.1B of direct wages before benefits and overhead.
pools.money_flow: Plants pay their own maintenance staff and outsourced repair shops and contractors to keep production equipment (motors, pumps, gearboxes, conveyors, machine tools) running.
pools.shock: BLS 2025-35 projections: +14% (78,900 jobs, to about 626,200), about 51,900 openings a year, much faster than average [primary; release month inferred]. Deloitte/Manufacturing Institute (April 2024): up to 3.8M manufacturing jobs needed by 2033 with 1.9M possibly unfilled. Reshoring and automation enlarge the installed base to maintain (North American robot orders 36,766 units in 2025).
pools.incumbents: In-house plant maintenance departments (most of the money); OEM service arms (Siemens, ABB, Rockwell); regional motor, pump and gearbox rebuilders; maintenance contractors and industrial staffing firms (the latter from memory).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fragmented owner-led repair shops, technician scarcity, knowledge held by retiring workers, and OEM service lock-in on proprietary controls; none can scale labor quickly.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Sensing and AI is funded: Augury ($75M Series F, Feb 2025, valuation above $1B); Tractian ($120M Series C, late 2024); competitors named in lists include MachineMetrics, Falkonry, Uptake, Uptime AI; Fullbay (truck-shop software) is adjacent. No funded startup selling technician labor or repair capacity as a service to plants was found.
pools.wedge_hints: Technician-as-a-service with an apprenticeship pipeline and dispatch; motor, pump and gearbox rebuild roll-up with rebuild-versus-replace software (tariffs make replacement costlier); spare-part reverse engineering and remanufacture (DLA is doing this for DoD); outcome-priced maintenance bundled with sensing. Bottom-up check: $100M of labor-as-a-service needs about 800 technicians at $125k revenue each, about 0.15% of the workforce; the hard part is gross margin and recruiting.
pools.insider_roles: Plant maintenance managers; reliability engineers; maintenance planners and schedulers; motor-repair shop owners (EASA members); millwright union business agents; OEM field-service managers.

pools.name: Owners' parts and service spend on heavy equipment (ag, construction, mining), opened by right-to-repair
pools.size_basis: Floor figure: Caterpillar services revenues of about $24B in 2025 per Cat's 2026 proxy statement [secondary, via search summary; I could not reach the 10-K MD&A text to confirm, and I could not confirm a $28B 2026 services target]. Cat total 2025 sales and revenues $67.589B [primary, 10-K]. Deere, CNH, AGCO, Komatsu and Kubota aftermarket is on top; I did not retrieve Deere's parts-and-service total.
pools.money_flow: Farmers, contractors and miners pay OEM dealer networks for parts, diagnostics and repair; software locks (diagnostic tools, component pairing, emissions limp mode) have kept independent shops out.
pools.shock: On 2026-07-08 the FTC and five states (Illinois, Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin) announced a settlement with Deere: a 10-year order requiring the same repair resources Deere gives dealers (read, clear and reset fault codes, reprogram and pair components, restart after emissions shutdown, manuals and troubleshooting) to farmers and independent shops on fair and reasonable terms, with no dealer retaliation; no fee schedule; stipulated order filed in N.D. Illinois and pending judicial approval. Preceded by a $99M class settlement in April 2026 in which Deere also promised digital repair tools for 10 years, starting before end-2026.
pools.incumbents: OEMs and franchised dealer networks (Deere, Caterpillar, CNH, AGCO, Komatsu); parts and service carry higher margins than new machines (from memory) and are captured through proprietary software and dealer exclusivity.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: dealer service departments are profit centers protected by franchise law, so an OEM cannot price tools low without cannibalising dealers, yet 'fair and reasonable terms' is now court-enforced for Deere. The order covers Deere ag equipment only; Cat and construction/mining brands are not parties.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found. Searches for 2026 funding of multi-brand diagnostic or independent-shop software for ag and construction equipment returned nothing; the settlement is only three months old, so absence may reflect search limits. Adjacent but not equivalent: truck-shop software Fullbay.
pools.wedge_hints: Multi-brand diagnostic hardware and software for independent ag and construction repair shops (the Snap-on/Autel-for-tractors analogy); mobile field-repair networks; remanufactured emissions and electronic components; shop-management and parts cross-reference software; extended warranty and financing for independents. Legal premise: order unapproved as of the FTC page, pricing not final, Deere-only; construction and mining depend on state laws and DMCA repair exemptions (from memory). Bottom-up check: 5% of a Cat-scale $24B pool at a 10% take is $120M, with heroic share-shift assumptions.
pools.insider_roles: Independent ag and construction repair shop owners; former Deere and Cat dealer service managers; custom-harvester and large-fleet equipment managers; equipment auction appraisers; US PIRG right-to-repair staff.

pools.name: North American manufacturers' spend on factory-automation and robot cells (robots plus integration)
pools.size_basis: My estimate. A3: North American companies ordered 36,766 robots worth $2.25B in 2025 (+6.6% units, +10.1% revenue; 2024: 31,311 units). Using a rule of thumb that the robot is about 25% of installed cell cost (from memory), $2.25B x 4 is about $9B. Cross-check: Control Engineering's 2026 Giants list shows the top 75 integrators alone reporting $4.67B of integration revenue net of hardware, +18% year on year (secondary, voluntary self-reporting).
pools.money_flow: Manufacturers pay robot OEMs (FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, KUKA), controls vendors (Rockwell, Siemens) and system integrators for robot cells and automation projects.
pools.shock: Commerce opened a Section 232 investigation into robotics and industrial machinery in September 2025; by mid-2026 the administration signalled new tariffs but no final action was found; a 2026-06-01 proclamation cut Section 232 rates on ag, mobile industrial and HVAC equipment (effective 2026-06-08 through 2027-12-31). Demand is rotating: H1-2026 North American robot orders were 17,995 units and $1.166B (+2.0% units, +6.6% value) with semiconductors/electronics +35%, pharma +32%, automotive components +24% and automotive OEMs -25%.
pools.incumbents: Robot OEMs (FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, KUKA), controls vendors (Rockwell, Siemens) and thousands of custom-engineering system integrators; integrators with over $100M gross revenue rose from 12% in 2021 to 24% in 2025.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Integrators are labor-bound project shops with scarce controls engineers (average engineers per integrator 105 in 2021, 168 in 2025), quote each project by hand, and face tariff-driven equipment cost inflation and pricing pressure.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Standard Bots ($200M Series C June 2026, $1B valuation; Sacra estimates $24M ARR in 2025); Vention ($110M Series D, Jan 2026); Path Robotics ($100M Series D, Oct 2024); Bright Machines ($126M Series C, June 2024); Formic (tiny listed round); Hadrian for machining cells. Figures are from aggregators, not company releases.
pools.wedge_hints: Integrator back-office and engineering tools (quoting, PLC and cell-code generation, commissioning); brownfield welding and machine-tending for small shops; used and refurbished robot resale; safety validation services. Watch the pending Section 232 robotics outcome.
pools.insider_roles: Integrator project managers and controls engineers; plant automation engineers; robot-brand distributors; machine builders; safety assessors.

pools.name: US importers' customs-duty payments on industrial inputs and the duty-mitigation services market
pools.size_basis: About $214B of US customs duties over the trailing twelve months through July 2026, from a tracker of Monthly Treasury Statement data (secondary; I did not open the Treasury statement; net monthly figures can dip when duties are refunded). The capturable services fee pool (brokers, counsel, drawback, audits) is a small fraction and was not sized. Overlap flag: finance slice excluded IEEPA refund claims; this pool is duties on Section 232 and 301 goods and the mitigation services.
pools.money_flow: Importers pay duties to CBP, and pay customs brokers, trade counsel and consultants for classification, valuation, origin, drawback and foreign-trade-zone work.
pools.shock: Section 122 surcharge expired 2026-07-24; Section 301 duties (10% or 12.5%) on goods from 60 economies took effect 2026-07-23 with no statutory sunset and a pending court challenge; Section 232 stacks on top; the formal derivative-inclusions process ended 2026-04-06; IEEPA tariffs were struck down 2026-02-20 and the Court of International Trade ordered refunds with interest in early March 2026. Customs bonds, audits and enforcement are rising.
pools.incumbents: Customs brokers (UPS, Expeditors, Livingston and others, from memory), Big Four and trade-law firms, and trade-software vendors (E2open and similar, from memory); a CBP trade-enforcement tool contract lists Altana as incumbent on the government side.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Hourly-billing brokers and counsel are built for stable rules; tariff stacking changes monthly and classification and origin work is manual and error-prone.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Altana (about $323-337M total raised, $1B valuation July 2024); Tarifflo (YC S26; AuditLive recovers overpaid duty; $500K+ pre-seed); Tariff Sense (Canada, CAD 220k pre-seed Dec 2025); TariffLens AI (launched May 2026); traide AI (Berlin); Flexport is also active (from memory). Many AI classification entrants but little capital outside Altana.
pools.wedge_hints: Post-entry audits and recovery of overpaid Section 232/301 duties on a contingency basis; first-sale-for-export and drawback programs for mid-market manufacturers; metals-content declarations for Section 232 derivatives (the 15%-by-weight carve-out and annex treatment make this a real data task); supplier origin evidence. Legal premise: contingency fees on duty recovery need a licensed customs broker or counsel in the loop; refund eligibility turns on the 180-day protest window and 2026 court orders.
pools.insider_roles: Licensed customs brokers; import compliance managers at mid-size manufacturers; trade counsel; CBP import specialists; drawback specialists.

pools.name: US medium- and heavy-duty truck parts aftermarket bought by independent fleets and shops
pools.size_basis: IBISWorld: about $25.5B of 2026 sales through US heavy-duty truck parts dealers (dealers only, so a floor) [secondary]. Global heavy-duty aftermarket estimates range $93B-$158B, with North America about 36% of the heavy-duty automotive aftermarket, but definitions differ and no clean US independent-aftermarket figure was found.
pools.money_flow: Fleets and owner-operators pay dealers, distributors and independent shops for engine, drivetrain, brake and chassis parts and repair.
pools.shock: 25% Section 232 tariff on imported medium- and heavy-duty trucks and truck parts (Class 3-8, engines, transmissions, tires, chassis), proclaimed 2025-10-17 and effective 2025-11-01; USMCA-eligible goods are treated on non-US content; manufacturer offsets of 3.75% benefit domestic assemblers, not aftermarket importers. FreightWaves reports heavy-duty engine parts cost 20-30% more than two years ago and many small carriers have not changed how they buy parts (unverified).
pools.incumbents: OEM dealers (PACCAR Parts, Volvo/Mack, Daimler Truck), national distributors (FleetPride, TruckPro and others, from memory) and independent repair shops.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Price discovery is by phone and parts counter, sourcing is concentrated in imports now taxed, and small fleets buy through habit, so dealers and distributors cannot easily offer transparent multi-source pricing.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Fullbay (heavy-duty shop-management software, $23M growth round July 2024 from JMI Equity with Mainsail; reported acquisition of Pitstop in March 2026, unverified); Decisiv (service software, not researched). No funded heavy-duty parts-procurement startup found.
pools.wedge_hints: Parts price transparency and sourcing for small fleets and independent shops, including tariff-avoiding sources; remanufactured and domestic alternatives to taxed imports; core-return and warranty-recovery services; parts availability for down trucks. Bottom-up check: 1% of $25.5B is $255M of parts flow, so $100M of revenue needs about 0.4% of dealer-channel flow at full pass-through or about 4% at a 10% take.
pools.insider_roles: Parts counter managers at truck dealers and distributors; independent fleet maintenance managers; owner-operators; heavy-duty shop owners; Auto Care Association and HDMA staff.

pools.name: US-owned and foreign OEM contract manufacturing in Mexico (IMMEX / maquila) under the USMCA review
pools.size_basis: More than $300B of IMMEX goods shipped in 2024 (an export value, not a fee pool; value added in Mexico is lower and was not found). As of December 2025: 6,512 active IMMEX establishments, 3.15M workers, monthly revenues above 653B pesos [secondary, American Industries Group; sources disagree on IMMEX's share of exports, 40% of total vs about 80% of manufacturing exports].
pools.money_flow: US and foreign OEMs pay Mexican export-manufacturing operations (their own plants, shelter operators, EMS firms) to build products under the IMMEX duty-deferral program; customs brokers, industrial-park developers and compliance providers earn fees around it.
pools.shock: The first USMCA joint review closed on 2026-07-01 without the 16-year extension, moving the three countries to annual reviews (the agreement itself runs to 2036); US-Mexico bilateral rounds covered steel, aluminum, autos, labor and rules of origin (third round ended about 2026-07-23, fourth set for Washington in September 2026; auto rules of origin unresolved). TrendForce says nearshoring investment turned more cautious; the Wilson Center found most sourcing changes made to meet rules of origin raised cost.
pools.incumbents: EMS and contract manufacturers (Jabil, Flex, Foxconn, Celestica, Plexus, from memory), shelter operators, industrial-park developers and customs brokers.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Plants with multi-year paybacks now sit on a one-year political horizon; rules-of-origin changes can strand compliance work; many nearshore operations are limited assembly that the review will sort from genuine production.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found. Searches for 2025-2026 funding of Mexico contract-manufacturing or USMCA rules-of-origin platforms returned only vendor marketing; incumbent software (E2open) and ERP add-ons (a 2026 NetSuite USMCA guide) cover part of the problem. Evidence of absence is weak.
pools.wedge_hints: USMCA origin and regional-value-content evidence collection across supplier tiers (a data-chasing task that recurs with every annual review); shelter-as-a-service for mid-size US manufacturers; Mexico-side quality and inspection services; dual-footprint (Mexico plus US) planning tools. Payer and budget line are weakest here, so treat as the least promising of the ten.
pools.insider_roles: Mexican customs brokers (agentes aduanales); IMMEX program administrators; maquila plant managers; USMCA compliance managers at OEMs; industrial-park brokers.

pools.name: US CRE borrowers' refinancing, extension and transaction costs on the loan maturity wall
pools.size_basis: MBA: $875B of commercial/multifamily mortgages mature in 2026 (17% of $5.0T; $957B in 2025, $652B in 2027). My derivation of the fee pool: ~$700-800B annual originations (MBA ~$706B in 2025; ~$806B forecast 2026) x 1.0-1.5% all-in friction (broker/banker, lender fee, legal, appraisal, reports, title) = $7-12B, plus ~$0.5-1B extension/modification fees on ~$200B extended. Central estimate $9B. Sanity check: Walker & Dunlop booked $1.2B revenue on $54.8B volume in 2025.
pools.money_flow: Borrowers pay capital-markets brokers/bankers, lender origination fees, lawyers, appraisers, title and report vendors to refinance or extend; lenders pay special servicers when loans default. Signers: borrower CFO/principal; bank chief credit officer or workout head.
pools.shock: MBA Feb 2026 survey shows $875B maturing in 2026 and lenders no longer simply extending (First American: extensions fell from $384B in 2024-25 to $200B in 2025-26). Trepp Sept 2026: CMBS delinquency 8.02% (highest since late 2020), office 12.16%, multifamily 8.04%; special servicing 10.86% overall and 16.75% office (May 2026).
pools.incumbents: Capital-markets brokers and bankers (CBRE, JLL, Newmark, Cushman, Berkadia, Walker & Dunlop; only W&D verified in this pass), banks holding $396B of the maturing debt, CMBS servicers/special servicers, debt funds (CRE private credit took 23% of capital raised in Q1 2026, secondary). Fees are mostly success-based commissions.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Low to moderate. Large brokers hold relationships and the fee pool is largely captured by them. Softness is in sub-$10M loans at community and regional banks, which are manual and local; a software-only entrant faces the problem that the lender, not the borrower, controls the decision.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Atlas Invest (AI-driven CRE bridge lender, $25M led by BlackRock Jan 2026, $38M total); Blooma (AI underwriting for lenders, $15M Series A 2021, older). Found no 2025-26 round for Lev or a refinance marketplace in 3 searches. Private credit capital is heavy even though venture-funded software is thin.
pools.wedge_hints: Sub-$10M loan workflow for community banks (collateral re-underwriting, extension/modification paperwork); borrower-side refinance readiness packages for small owners; special-servicing workout administration for bank-held (non-CMBS) loans.
pools.insider_roles: CRE debt brokers, bank workout officers, special servicer asset managers, receivers, appraisers valuing distressed office.

pools.name: US homeowners-insurer-paid property repair and restoration (claims money flowing to contractors)
pools.size_basis: III (verified): 2025 net premiums earned $152.6B; incurred losses 53.6% of premiums = ~$82B; loss plus LAE 61.1% = ~$93B. ISO 2023: property damage 97.3% of claims (wind/hail 42.5%, water 22.6%, fire 21.6%), so the claim money is overwhelmingly repair/rebuild spend. LA fires alone: CA Dept of Insurance says >$22.4B paid on 42,121 claims (secondary).
pools.money_flow: Insurers pay claim proceeds, often by check jointly payable to homeowner and mortgage servicer (loss draft), which flow to roofers, restoration contractors, GCs and public adjusters; carriers also pay adjusters, TPAs and estimating software. Signers: restoration/roofing contractor owner; servicer loss-draft operations head; carrier claims-ops VP.
pools.shock: Jan 2025 Los Angeles wildfires (largest payout event), plus 2025-26 shift to actual-cash-value/payment-schedule roof settlements. Verisk 2026 roof report (secondary): roof claims fell ~20% in 2025 but average roof replacement hit $17,631 (+33% vs 2021-24). Texas TDI clarified 2026-09-29 that insurers may weigh roof condition.
pools.incumbents: Carriers; Verisk (Xactware/Xactimate) and Cotality for estimating; Sedgwick and Crawford as TPAs/adjusters; restoration franchisors; public adjusters (vendor names other than Sedgwick not re-verified). Mortgage servicers control loss-draft release (Fannie/Freddie thresholds per a Louisiana AG summary: <=$20k to borrower alone, >$20k joint with contractor, licensed contractor at $40k+; verify against Selling Guides). ~60% of owner-occupied homes carry a mortgage (ACS 2022, secondary).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Contractor base is fragmented and cash-constrained; carrier payment rules are changing (ACV roofs, schedules); the servicer loss-draft step is a manual back office. Carriers resist tools that raise payouts, so contractor-side products need to be paid by contractors.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Rebuild (restoration claims software, $13M Series A Sept 2026 led by Asymmetric Capital Partners; $2.1M seed Jan 2025); NovaData Solutions (carrier-side restoration invoice review, Series A Mar 2024, Activate Venture Partners); Xcelerate (restoration documentation software); T&M Pro (acquired by Sedgwick).
pools.wedge_hints: Contractor cash acceleration against approved claims; recoverable-depreciation holdback recovery on ACV roofs; servicer-side loss-draft disbursement and inspection workflow; contents inventory; post-catastrophe lien and payment tracking.
pools.insider_roles: Restoration estimators and owners, public adjusters, mortgage servicer loss-draft managers, roofing contractor owners, carrier claims-operations leaders.

pools.name: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
pools.geography: United States (Florida and California are the largest concentrations)
pools.size_basis: FCAR 2025 Statistical Review (verified PDF): $124.2B of assessments collected in 2025, of which $31.1B contributed to reserve funds; 373,000 associations; 35.2% of US housing; 9,000-10,000 management companies; 30-40% self-managed; Florida 50,600 associations / 4.47M units.
pools.money_flow: Owners pay assessments to associations, which pay management companies, insurers, utilities, landscapers and contractors, and fund reserves for roofs, elevators, structure and pools. Signers: board treasurer/president on owner votes (Florida allows loans and lines of credit with majority owner approval), advised by the management company.
pools.shock: Fannie Mae Lender Letter LL-2026-03 (Mar 18, 2026): minimum reserve allocation rises from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income for loan applications dated on/after Jan 4, 2027; Limited Review ended for established projects >10 units (Aug 3, 2026 per summaries). Buildings that miss the floor lose conventional financing eligibility. Florida: reserves must be funded to 100% of structural-integrity study recommendations from Jan 1, 2026 with no waiver (HB 913, 2025); Miami Realtors found 62% of South Florida associations missed the original Dec 31, 2024 study deadline. Fannie PDF returned 403; five secondary summaries agree.
pools.incumbents: Management companies (9,000-10,000 firms), reserve-study firms (Association Reserves, Reserve Advisors), portfolio banks that lend to associations (e.g. U.S. Century Bank in Miami), insurers writing master policies.
pools.incumbent_fragility: 30-40% of associations are volunteer-run; boards face a hard compliance deadline with six-figure per-unit exposure in some Florida buildings; conventional unit-owner financing is tightening; association lending is bank-local and slow.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Vantaca (HOA management software, $300M+ growth round at $1.25B Oct 2025, Cove Hill Partners; 500+ management companies, 6M households); PayHOA ($27.5M Series A May 2024); Assembly HOA ($1.8M); Bluejay HOA ($2.0M). Found no venture-scale startup in association capital-project financing or procurement.
pools.wedge_hints: Special-assessment financing and loan servicing for Florida condo associations (lien-secured); 15%-rule budget modeling and lender-eligibility reporting; milestone-inspection repair project procurement; master-policy premium financing.
pools.insider_roles: Community association managers, reserve specialists, condo attorneys, association lending officers at community banks, engineers performing milestone inspections, insurance brokers placing master policies.

pools.name: US third-party property management fees and rent-pricing software
pools.size_basis: Census via FRED: total revenue of real estate property managers (NAICS 53131, employer firms) was $105.2B in 2022 (up from $94.3B in 2021). Includes non-residential managers; no Census residential-only series found. 60,818 residential property manager establishments in 2023 (third-party summary of Census data). A $134.2B figure for NAICS 531311 is unverified.
pools.money_flow: Owners pay property managers (management fees, leasing and maintenance markups) and software vendors (property management systems, revenue management). Signers: regional VP of operations or head of revenue management at an operator; asset manager at an owner.
pools.shock: DOJ-RealPage proposed consent decree (Nov 2025): no real-time use of competitors' nonpublic data, training data at least one year old, no features limiting price decreases. Greystar, Cortland, LivCor and Willow Bridge settled; 10 states still litigating; Maryland HB 434 and Massachusetts H.5222 (2026) pending. Also the Jan 20, 2026 executive order restricting federal financing support for large institutional single-family buyers (build-to-rent carved out; Invitation Homes fell 7.5%).
pools.incumbents: RealPage, Yardi, AppFolio, Entrata and large operators' in-house teams (names from background knowledge, not re-verified). Fragmented small managers underneath.
pools.incumbent_fragility: The dominant revenue-management product is now legally constrained in its core mechanism (pooled competitor data). Small and mid-size landlords lack compliant pricing options.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: EliseAI ($250M Series E Aug 2025 at ~$2.2B; $350M at $4B Sept 2026; reported >$200M ARR by June 2026; secondary); Latchel ($16.7M Series A 2022, Allegion Ventures 2023, single-family maintenance); Belong ($50M total). AI leasing and resident communication is the generic-copilot trap.
pools.wedge_hints: Compliant public-data-only market benchmarking and pricing for small and mid-size landlords; maintenance coordination and turn operations for single-family and build-to-rent operators; audit trails for pricing recommendations.
pools.insider_roles: Revenue managers, regional property managers, antitrust counsel at operators, single-family maintenance operations heads.

pools.name: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
pools.geography: United States (Florida, Texas, California, Tennessee lead on private-provider laws)
pools.size_basis: My derivation: BLS counts ~133,640 construction and building inspectors (May 2023, mean wage $72,880) and ~147,600 jobs in 2024 (OOH, median $72,120) = ~$10-11B in inspector wages alone, excluding plan examiners, permit technicians, software, overhead and private-provider fees. Context: Census Aug 2026 private residential construction $882B SAAR, total $2.2T.
pools.money_flow: Applicants pay permit, plan-review and inspection fees to cities and counties; under private-provider laws they pay licensed third-party reviewers/inspectors directly. Signers: builder/contractor permit coordinator or owner; city building official or CIO.
