pools.shock: State laws moving work to private providers when governments miss deadlines: Florida HB 803 (signed May 6, 2026, effective July 1, 2026) sets a 10-business-day clock with private providers (5 for single-trade single-family work), deemed approval on a miss, and reported 50% commercial permit-fee cut when private providers do all review and inspection; California AB 253 (signed Oct 10, 2025) allows third-party review after 30 days; Texas HB 14 (2023) and SB 1450 (2025); Tennessee Public Chapter 771 (2024); Florida HB 683 (2025).
pools.incumbents: Municipal building departments, permitting-system vendors (Tyler Technologies, Accela, Clariti; vendors other than Clariti from background knowledge), code-consulting and third-party review firms.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Public departments are understaffed and statutory clocks now shift volume to private providers faster than departments can hire; permit software vendors sell to the same governments losing volume.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: PermitFlow ($54M Series B Dec 2025 led by Accel; ~$90M total); CivCheck (AI plan review, acquired by Clariti; Honolulu requires it for eligible residential projects from Sept 1, 2026; Denver uses it). No venture-backed licensed private-provider firm combining software and a state inspection license was found.
pools.wedge_hints: Licensed private provider (plan review plus inspection) in FL/TX/CA/TN earning the review and inspection fee with software doing first-pass checks; single-trade permits (solar, HVAC, roofing, electrical) where the shortest clocks apply; inspection scheduling for builders.
pools.insider_roles: Building officials, plan examiners, ICC-certified private providers, permit expediters, builder permit coordinators.

pools.name: US residential construction trade labor (payroll and subcontract labor, plus staffing/payroll/training intermediation)
pools.size_basis: My derivation from BLS (Sept 2026): residential building construction 922.7k + residential specialty trade contractors 2,340.3k = 3.26M jobs; construction average weekly earnings $1,634.25 (~$85k/yr; all-construction payroll ~$710B on 8.364M jobs); at ~$75k for residential trades, payroll is ~$245B. Intermediation layer (staffing, PEO/payroll, workers' comp, recruiting, training) at 5-15% = $12-37B. NAHB (ACS 2024, secondary): immigrants 26.3% of construction workforce; ~1.5M undocumented (Pew via secondary).
pools.money_flow: Builders and remodelers pay framers, drywallers, roofers, concrete and finish crews directly or through subcontractors; intermediaries take a share. Signers: residential contractor owner or builder field-operations VP.
pools.shock: AGC/NCCER 2026 Workforce Survey (released Sept 3, 2026; 1,830 respondents, primary): 87% have craft openings, 50% of those say harder to fill; ~29% report an immigration-enforcement effect in six months (42% in the South); 16% say subcontractors lost workers; 42% say labor shortages delayed projects; >80% raised base pay; 36% increased training spend; 49% expanded online recruiting; data centers pull skilled labor.
pools.incumbents: General staffing firms, union hiring halls and apprenticeship trusts, local labor brokers and informal 1099 crews, PEOs.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Informal labor supply is exposed to I-9/E-Verify risk and enforcement, which is the shock; no incumbent specializes in compliant residential crew supply. Legal premise to check: worker classification, E-Verify duties and joint-employer liability for a platform placing crews.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Buildforce ($10M Series A July 28, 2026 led by Saepio Capital; commercial electrician staffing). None found for residential framing, drywall, roofing or concrete crews in 3 searches; labor marketplaces have a poor track record (misclassification, thin margins), so 'open' reflects a thin search and a hard model.
pools.wedge_hints: Verified-work-authorization crew staffing for builders; training-to-placement pipelines paid by contractors; payroll, certified-payroll and workers' compensation bundles for small subcontractors.
pools.insider_roles: Residential framing and drywall subcontractors, builder field-operations VPs, union apprenticeship coordinators, immigration and employment counsel, workers' compensation brokers.

pools.name: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
pools.size_basis: My derivation: MHI April 2026 report (read): seasonally adjusted annual shipments 103,703; YTD through April 33,054 (-7.3%); 57.7% multi-section. Census prices (secondary): new single-section ~$88-91k, double-section ~$161-164k, excluding land, delivery and setup. Blended ~$131k x ~104k homes = ~$13.6B. FHFA says chattel loans are 70-80% of new manufactured homes, so ~$9-11B chattel originations. Lot rent is a separate stream (MHI: >43,000 communities, ~4.3M homesites), not included.
pools.money_flow: Buyers pay manufacturers, retail dealers and installers; most finance with chattel loans from specialized lenders; many homes sit on leased lots paying lot rent. Signers: buyer via dealer; dealer principal for lender partnerships; chattel lender CEO for servicing/securitization.
pools.shock: June 2026 rule proposals: FHFA proposed replacing Duty to Serve with an outcome framework emphasizing chattel loans (91 FR 37848, published June 24, 2026; final expected effective by Jan 1, 2028); HUD proposed June 12, 2026 to require the permanent chassis only for lowest-floor sections, enabling multistory homes (HUD est. $4,800-6,700 saved per multistory unit; comment closed Aug 11, 2026; not final). ICBA opposes GSE expansion under conservatorship.
pools.incumbents: Clayton (Berkshire; 21st Mortgage, Vanderbilt), Cavco, Skyline Champion (names from background knowledge, not re-verified); chattel lenders; community owners including private equity (Florida, Michigan, Texas heavy).
pools.incumbent_fragility: GSEs do not buy chattel loans, so lenders charge high rates and portfolio their loans; a GSE chattel channel would reprice the market. Lot-rent disputes and state bills pressure community owners.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Zippy (digital chattel lender, $26M total, last reported July 2023); CoverTree (manufactured-home insurance, $13M Series A May 2024); Tammac Holdings ($60M debt and equity, undated); Apollo manufactured-housing fund ($850M first close late 2025, institutional not a startup). Few venture-funded players found.
pools.wedge_hints: Chattel origination and servicing platform built to GSE standards so loans become securitizable; conversion finance for resident-owned communities; land-lease home insurance and escrow; dealer-side finance workflow.
pools.insider_roles: Manufactured-home retail dealership managers, chattel underwriters and servicers, community operators, state manufactured housing association executives, plant managers, installers.

pools.name: US new-home builder sales incentives and mortgage rate buydowns
pools.size_basis: My derivation: Census 679,000 new homes sold in 2025; Dec 2025 median $414,400; Lennar FY2025 ASP $391,000 => ~$270B annual new-home sales. Lennar said it held ~14% in incentives and price adjustments in Q4 2025 (company release, read); Pulte incentives 10.9% of gross price in Q1 2026 vs 8% a year earlier (secondary); NAHB Sept 2026: two-thirds of builders use incentives, 38% cut prices by avg 6%. At a blended 8-10% the pool is ~$24B (range $16-38B); only the buydown/closing-credit share reaches third parties and I did not find that split.
pools.money_flow: Builders give buyers price cuts, closing credits and rate buydowns; buydown dollars are paid to lenders, often the builder's captive mortgage company. Signers: builder CFOs and heads of mortgage joint ventures.
pools.shock: Incentive intensity rose sharply in late 2025-2026 as new-home inventory built (Lennar ~14%, Dec 16, 2025 release; Lennar guided Q1 2026 gross margin 15-16% vs 18.7% a year earlier). Regulators are watching: Feb 2026 Benesch alert warns promotional rates can mask higher prices; an analysis cited by CUNY coverage found ~20.8% of D.R. Horton and ~30.7% of Lennar FHA loans underwater (secondary, verify).
pools.incumbents: Builder captive lenders: Lennar Financial Services earned $612.5M operating profit in FY2025 (company release); D.R. Horton and Pulte captives (background knowledge). Many incentive packages require the captive lender (Texas buydown guide, secondary).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Incentives are eroding builder gross margins, captive steering faces regulatory scrutiny, and mid-size builders without captives have no neutral buydown capital or administration option. Legal premise to check: seller-concession caps (FHA ~6%, VA ~4%, conventional 3-9% by LTV; from background knowledge, must be verified), RESPA steering, appraisal treatment.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found for builder-side buydown pricing, escrow, insurance or hedging (3 searches). Adjacent and older only: Built Technologies (construction lending software), UpEquity (2021 cash-offer rounds).
pools.wedge_hints: Independent buydown pricing and escrow administration for mid-size builders without captives; forward-commitment capital for temporary buydowns; compliance and disclosure audit tooling.
pools.insider_roles: Builder CFOs, captive mortgage heads, builder closing managers, FHA underwriters, settlement agents.

pools.name: US title insurance premiums and settlement
pools.size_basis: ALTA market share analysis (via ALTA release coverage): 2024 title insurance premiums $16.2B, up 7% from 2023; claims paid ~$676M (~4% of premiums). Shares: First American 22.2%, Fidelity National 14.3%, Old Republic 14.3%, Chicago Title 13.4% (Fidelity-owned), Stewart 9.2%.
pools.money_flow: Buyers and lenders pay title premiums through agents, who keep most of the premium and remit a share to underwriters; settlement/escrow fees are additional. Signers: lender secondary-marketing/QC head for waiver-based products; title agent for closing software.
pools.shock: FHFA/Fannie Mae title waiver pilot lets qualifying refinances (LTV under 80%) be sold without a lender title policy or attorney opinion letter; expanded July 2025 with a second vendor (Westcor); Pulte says more expansion coming; pilot scheduled to end Nov 30, 2027. ALTA opposes (fraud ~40% of refinance title claim cost); H.R. 5837 would require title insurance on all GSE loans. No 2026 rule or rate data found.
pools.incumbents: Four underwriter groups hold ~70% of premiums; they own agencies and technology (Endpoint is a First American subsidiary with $220M raised from its parent).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fragile on lender policies in refinances, not on owner's policies in purchases. The pilot is a regulatory bet that Congress or a new FHFA director could reverse, so the legal premise is weak.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Qualia (closing platform; $1B-plus valuation in 2020; an unverified aggregator lists a $50M round Sept 2026); Westcor (waiver pilot vendor); Endpoint (parent-funded). Could not verify 2025-26 rounds for Qualia or Pavaso.
pools.wedge_hints: Property-data risk scoring to qualify refinances for waiver; lender-side title quality-control tooling. Honest read: depends on a reversible pilot.
pools.insider_roles: Title agents and escrow officers, underwriting counsel, lender secondary-marketing and QC heads, title claims counsel.

pools.name: US low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) equity, development and compliance
pools.size_basis: Novogradac estimate of LIHTC equity market ~$25B in 2025, banks ~80% of equity in 2024 (cited in a June 2026 comment letter; secondary, PDF returned 403). Berkadia closed a $100M multi-investor LIHTC fund in Sept 2025.
pools.money_flow: Investors (mostly banks) buy federal tax credits from developers, funding construction/rehab of affordable rentals; property managers then run annual income certifications and compliance for 15+ years. Signers: state housing finance agency allocators, developers, bank CRA/tax-credit officers, owners.
pools.shock: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 2025) made permanent from 2026: private-activity-bond test for 4% deals falls from 50% to 25% (bonds issued after Dec 31, 2025) and 9% allocations rise 12%. Novogradac estimates ~1.22M additional affordable rentals over 2026-2035 (~$15.7B added housing credit investment). Open risks: lower equity pricing as volume rises, a June 2026 bank regulatory-capital proposal (details unverified), uncertain HUD rental assistance.
pools.incumbents: Syndicators and investors (Boston Capital, Raymond James, Enterprise; background knowledge), banks, state agencies, compliance monitoring firms and CPA firms such as Novogradac.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Bond-test change creates structuring work incumbents handle by hand; compliance and income recertification are labor-intensive; bank-dominated equity concentrates risk if capital rules change.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Pronto Housing (affordable housing compliance SaaS, ~$9M total, last round Feb 2024). No LIHTC marketplace or structuring startup found in 2 searches.
pools.wedge_hints: Income-certification and compliance automation for affordable properties; 25%-test structuring and pricing analytics for developers; credit and equity pricing data product; transfer marketplace. Revenue path: 1% of a $25B equity market is $250M, but the market is dominated by bank relationships, so $100M is a stretch.
pools.insider_roles: Syndicator asset managers, state allocators, tax-credit attorneys and CPAs, affordable-housing compliance specialists, bank CRA officers.
